Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 49, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

Surah al-Hujurat (The Chambers)

It is Medinan, as al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ikrimah and others said. In Majma' al-Bayan it is related from Ibn 'Abbas that it is Medinan except for one verse, which is His saying, ﴿O mankind, We created you from male and female﴾. Perhaps the one who takes into account what al-Hakim recorded in his Mustadrak, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and al-Bazzar in his Musnad, by way of al-A'mash from 'Alqamah from 'Abd Allah, who said: "What began with (O you who believe) was revealed in Medina, and what began with (O mankind) was in Mecca," (he means it is Meccan), without exception. The truth is that this is not a consistent rule.

al-Khafaji mentioned that it is Meccan according to an anomalous opinion, and it has eighteen verses by consensus. It is not hidden that it harmonizes with what precedes it, since both are Medinan and both contain rulings. The previous surah contains fighting against the disbelievers, and this one contains fighting against rebels. The previous one ends with (those who believe), and this one opens with (those who believe). The previous one contains honours bestowed upon him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, especially at its beginning, and this one also contains at its beginning kinds of honour for him, upon him be prayers and peace.

In al-Bahr, its connection with the end of what precedes it is evident, because He, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his companions, then He, glorified be He, said ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, etc. Thus it may happen that a believer who does righteous deeds commits something of which he should be forbidden. So He, exalted be He, said this as instruction to the believers and as refinement for them.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who believe, do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾. The opening of the address with the call (nida') is to alert the addressees that what falls within its scope is a grave matter that calls for their greater attention and excessive care in receiving and observing it. Describing them with faith is to encourage them and to indicate that it calls for guarding it and restrains from neglecting it.

(Tuqaddimu) is from qaddama, transitive. Its meaning is "to make a thing come forward," i.e., to be ahead of other things. Its expected construction would be to take two objects, but in usage it most commonly takes the second with (ʿalā), as you say: "I put so-and-so ahead of so-and-so." Here it admits of two possibilities:

The first is that its object is omitted, and the intention is the act itself, which is advancing, without regard to its being connected to any particular matter, and without considering what is being advanced, in the manner of His saying, ﴿He it is who gives life and causes death﴾, and their saying, "He gives and withholds." So the meaning is: do not perform advancing, do not engage in it, and do not make it a path for you.

The second is that its object is deliberately deleted in order to generalize it, because since it admits several matters, if one of them were specified it would be preference without a preponderating factor. So one supposes a general matter, since this conveys more with brevity. Thus the meaning is: do not put forward any matter whatsoever.

It has been said that the first is more suited to the context, because it conveys the prohibition against engaging in the act itself, which necessarily entails its complete non-existence, and this necessarily entails that its connection to its object does not exist, by the demonstrative method. The second has been preferred, on the grounds that it is more common in usage, and that in the first there is the treating of a transitive verb as intransitive, which goes against the basic principle, whereas the second is free of this. Deletion, though also contrary to the basic principle, is lighter than the aforementioned treatment, because it is more common in comparison. Some did not distinguish between them, because the preponderances conflicted in their view, and because both lead to the generality that suits the context.

It is mentioned that the sentence contains two figurative usages. One of them is in (bayna), since the literal sense of their saying (bayna yadayi fulan) is the space between the two hands. It is used figuratively for the two directions directly opposite a person's right and left, near him, by applying the term "two hands" to what adjoins them and faces them. So it is a metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal).

The second is the metaphor of the whole expression, namely "advancing between the two hands," which is an illustrative metaphor (istiʿara tamthiliyya) for issuing a ruling with certainty without following and imitating those whose imitation is required. It depicts its vileness and grotesqueness through the image of a perceptible thing in what they were forbidden, like a servant going ahead of his master on a journey where there is no benefit. So the meaning of ﴿do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾ is: do not decide a matter, firmly commit to it, and dare to perpetrate it before Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, have ruled and given permission for it. Its essence is the prohibition against undertaking any matter without modelling it on the examples of the Book and the Sunnah.

It is also permissible that (tuqaddimu) be from qadima, intransitive, meaning taqaddama, like wajjaha and bayyana. From this comes "the vanguard of the army," the opposite of its rear, which is the group in front of it. This is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Haywa, al-Dahhak, Ya'qub and Ibn Miqsam, "la taqaddamu," with a fatha on the ta', qaf and dal. Its original form was tatqaddamu, and one of the two ta's was deleted for lightness, because it is of the tafa''ala pattern, which is the intransitive reflexive. The former (the first reading) is preferred on account of what you have heard, and because it uses the more known and more famous of the two forms.

It might be objected: when the verb is governed by the adverbial complement, it may take the place of an object and thus convey generality, as they established in ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾. So let the adverb here stand in the place of the object of advancing, fulfilling its function. Advancing before a person is a departure from the quality of following in the perceptible sense, so it is more suitable to the illustrative metaphor, whose purpose is to depict the vileness of issuing a ruling without following and imitating those whose imitation is required, through the image of a perceptible thing. Thus the reading of (la tuqaddimu) as intransitive is more eloquent. The lack of fame does not harm it, for it does not compete with the eloquence that suits the context, in line with what was indicated in al-Kashshaf, that the intent is the prohibition against opposing the Book and the Sunnah. The transitive form indicates that this is by their making and intent to oppose, because advancing before a person is that you make someone, either yourself or another, go ahead before him. That is stronger in blame and more reprehensible, since it indicates a deliberate failure to follow, not its occurrence in any haphazard way. So understand this and do not be heedless.

It is also permissible that ﴿before Allah and His Messenger﴾ be of the type "Zayd pleased me, and his generosity." Then the prohibition is against advancing before the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, as if it were said: "Do not put yourselves forward before the Messenger of Allah." The mention of Allah, exalted be He, is to magnify him, upon him be prayers and peace, and to indicate the sublimity of his station with Him, Mighty and Majestic, and the greater specificity of his relation to Him, glorified be He. The matter of the figurative usage on this stays as it is. This is, as al-Kashshaf said, more suited to what comes after it, since the discourse is directed toward honouring him, upon him be prayers and peace. When the deserving of this honour is due to his being specially connected with Allah, exalted be He, and to his station with Him, glorified be He, then advancing before Allah, exalted be His glory, is more included in the prohibition and more apt. And if it is taken as intended in itself, as has passed, then the prohibition is against acting arbitrarily in a religious matter, not in every respect without referring to the Book and the Sunnah. On this is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas, as recorded by Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya from him, that he said: "That is, do not say anything contrary to the Book and the Sunnah." Likewise what Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from him, that he said: "They were forbidden to speak before his speech; rather they should listen and not speak."

The indication of this is that his speech, upon him be prayers and peace, is intended to be what he conveys from Him, Exalted, and its wording too, since the wording is from the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, even if the meaning is from revelation. Or it is intended that the speech of each of Allah, exalted be He, and the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, is meant. And what 'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, and others, recorded from Mujahid, that he said concerning this: "Do not forestall the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in anything until Allah decrees it through his tongue." This comes out along the lines of the first explanation of the words of Ibn 'Abbas and serves as its support. Some narrate that he said: "Do not forestall Allah, exalted be He, in anything until He relates it through the tongue of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace." This too was taken as support for the words of Ibn 'Abbas. The advancing before Allah, exalted be He, was interpreted in this way because advancing before the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, has a clear meaning. All of this is in the category of stating the general sense of the meaning.

In al-Durr al-Manthur, after mentioning what is narrated from Mujahid as we have related, the scholars of hadith (al-huffaz) said: "This interpretation is according to the reading (taqaddamu) with a fatha on the ta' and dal." It is a reading of some people, related by al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and others. It seems that this is based on the view that (tuqaddimu), in this reading, is from qadima, like ʿalima, meaning to proceed into war. It also comes from the pattern of nasara. For iftiyat, which is precedence without consulting the one who should be consulted, is more fitting for that.

Some eminent scholars chose to take it as from qadima meaning "to return from a journey," of the pattern ʿalima only, as the dictionary (al-Qamus) wording indicates. According to this, their haste in issuing a ruling on a matter of religion is likened to a traveller's arrival from his journey, indicating their intense eagerness for it, like ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾.

The occasion of revelation has been disputed. al-Bukhari, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "A party of Banu Tamim came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'Appoint al-Qa'qa' ibn Ma'bad.' 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'Rather, appoint al-Aqra' ibn Habis.' Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'You only intended to oppose me.' 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'I did not intend to oppose you.' They argued until their voices were raised. So Allah revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾ until the verse ends."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from al-Hasan that some people slaughtered before the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on the day of sacrifice, so he, upon him be prayers and peace, ordered them to repeat the slaughter. Then Allah revealed: ﴿O you who believe﴾ etc.

In al-Kashshaf it is related from him that some people slaughtered on the day of al-Adha before the prayer, so it was revealed, and he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered them to slaughter another. The first narration clearly indicates that the revelation came after the command and the slaughter before the prayer, and this entails that the slaughter took place before the Messenger of Allah, upon him be prayers and peace, because he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to slaughter after it, as the reports state. Abu Hanifa held that slaughter before it is not valid, and the reports support him. al-Shaykhan, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i recorded from al-Bara', who said: "Abu Burda ibn Niyar slaughtered before the prayer, so the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Replace it.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have nothing but a young goat (jadha'a).' He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Make it in its place, and it will not suffice for anyone after you.'"

In another narration, that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "The first thing we begin with on this day of ours is to pray, then return and slaughter. Whoever does this has hit our Sunnah, and whoever slaughters before that, it is merely meat he has provided for his family, and it is not part of the rite of sacrifice at all."

Abu Burda ibn Niyar had slaughtered before the prayer, and so on in the hadith. On this matter there is a lengthy discussion whose place is in the books of jurisprudence, so consult it if you wish.

Also from al-Hasan: when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, settled in Medina, delegations came to him from the horizons and asked him many questions. So they were forbidden to begin with a question, until he, upon him be prayers and peace, was the one who initiated.

Ibn Jarir and others recorded from Qatadah, who said: "It was related to us that some people used to say: 'If such-and-such had been revealed concerning such-and-such, it would have been such-and-such.' So Allah disliked that and forestalled it in this verse."

It was said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a sariyya (a raiding detachment) of twenty-seven men to Tihamah, under the command of al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr al-Sa'idi. The Banu 'Amir killed them, under the command of 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, except for three men who escaped. They met two men from the Banu Sulaym near Madinah, and they claimed affiliation to the Banu 'Amir, because they were more honored than Sulaym. So they killed the two and plundered them. Then they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'What a wretched thing you have done! They were from Sulaym, that is, they were from the people of the covenant, for they were under a pact. The plunder is what they were wearing, and he paid their blood-money.'" [Page 134] "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'And this was revealed': that is, 'Do not do anything on your own initiative until you seek the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'"

al-Tabarani related in al-Awsat, and Ibn Mardawayh, on the authority of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "Some people used to advance the month, fasting before the Prophet (ﷺ). So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾."

In another narration, on the authority of Masruq ibn al-Ajda' ibn Malik al-Hamdani al-Kufi, he said: "I entered upon 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and she had adopted him (as a fast) on the day about which there is doubt (about whether it is Ramadan). She said to the slave girl: 'Give him honey to drink.' I said: 'I am fasting.' She said: 'Allah the Exalted has forbidden fasting on this day, and it is concerning this that the verse was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not put forward...﴾' and so on." So the meaning, as in al-Ma'alim (Ma'alim al-Tanzil of al-Baghawi), is: "Do not fast before the fast of your Prophet."

Sahib al-Kashf (the author of al-Kashshaf) interpreted this, saying: "In my view, the apparent meaning is that she ('A'ishah) derived from the verse that the command and prohibition of the Prophet (ﷺ) should be obeyed. He (ﷺ) had forbidden it, and it was concerning this that the verse was revealed," that is, concerning the like of this, because it indicates the obligation of following and the prohibition of acting independently, since that interpretation does not apply to the day of doubt alone except with forced effort.

This is similar to what is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, in his answer to the woman who objected to him, saying that she had read the Book of Allah and had not found the curse upon the woman who tattoos. He, may Allah be pleased with him, said, as he claimed: "If you had read it, you would have found it. Have you not read: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Then he has forbidden it."

You know, after the first narration, this interpretation; and it is known from these narrations and others that they also differed in the interpretation of "advancing", and in many of them it is interpreted in a particular sense. Some of them said: the verse is general in every saying and action, and it includes that if a matter arises in the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they should not answer before him; that one should not walk in front of him except out of necessity; and that one should wait for him to begin the meal. This was preferred on the ground that it accords with the context, and with what is known in the principles of jurisprudence, that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the particularity of the cause. In speaking of it, according to what al-Tibi said, there is a metaphor (majaz) by way of the common element which also applies to the literal sense, not merely an illustration or the likening of an intelligible matter to a sensible one. In the principles it is called "generality of metaphor," and in the technical discipline it is called kinayah (metonymy), because it does not exclude the intended literal sense either. From here it is permissible to intend: "Do not walk in front of the Prophet (ﷺ)." May Allah have mercy on him, he mentioned that one cannot be a doer of this statement; rather the prohibition is directed at the act itself. So reflect.

The verse is cited as evidence for following the Shari'ah in everything, and this is evident from what has preceded. Perhaps the deniers of analogy (qiyas) have cited it, and, as al-Kiya said, this is false from them. Yes, al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: "It is cited as evidence for giving precedence to the explicit text over analogy," and perhaps this is based on the principle that acting on the explicit text is further from "advancing before Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ)."

﴿And fear Allah﴾, that is, in everything you do and abstain from, of sayings and actions, of which this matter under discussion is one. ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of everything heard, including your sayings, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of all that is known, including your actions. So it is His right that He be feared and that one be mindful of Him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 49, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾. This begins the prohibition against exceeding the bounds in the manner of speaking in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), after the prohibition against exceeding the bounds in speech and action themselves. The address "O you who have believed" is repeated, although the previous address is recent, for the sake of emphasis in alerting and admonishing, and to indicate that each of the two statements stands independently, calling for close attention to its matter. That is, do not let your voices go beyond the limit that he (ﷺ) reaches with his own voice.

Ibn Mas'ud recited "lā taraffa'ū bi-aṣwātikum", with the doubling of the ra' in "taraffa'ū" and the addition of the letter bāʾ. Al-A'lam al-Hudhali used the doubled form in his verse:

"I raised my eye towards the Hijaz, to people renowned for their virtues."

The doubling here serves emphasis, like the addition of the bāʾ in the recitation. However, the meaning is not that they were forbidden from a violent raising, imagining that what is less than violent would be permissible for them. Rather, the meaning is the prohibition against the uproar they were engaged in and their coarseness in what they were doing. This is similar to His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume usury, doubled and redoubled﴾.

﴿And do not speak to him loudly as you speak loudly to one another﴾, that is, with a loudness such as the loudness that occurs among yourselves. The first is a prohibition against raising the voice above his voice (ﷺ), and this is a prohibition against equating their loudness with his loudness (ﷺ), since that is what is customary in addressing equals and peers. From this it is understood that lowering the voice is obligatory, so that their voices are below his voice (ﷺ). It has been said that the first prohibition is specific to his speaking to them, and this is about his silence (ﷺ). It is as if it were said: do not raise your voices above his voice when he speaks and you speak, and do not speak loudly to him when he is silent and you speak. It is also understood that it is obligatory for their voices to be below his voice (ﷺ). Whichever interpretation is taken, the outcome is: make your voices lower than his voice (ﷺ), and be careful in addressing him to use a gentleness close to a whisper, as is the custom when addressing one who is awe-inspiring and revered. Observe the dignity of prophethood and the greatness of its station. For this reason Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), after the revelation of the verse, as ʿAbd ibn Humayd and al-Hakim related, and the latter declared sound, through the chain of Abu Salamah from Abu Hurayrah, said: "By the One who revealed the Book to you, O Messenger of Allah, I will not speak to you except as one who speaks in a whisper, until I meet Allah, the Exalted."

In another narration, he said: "O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, I will not speak to you except in a whisper, or like one who whispers, until I meet Allah, the Exalted." Whenever delegations came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he would send someone to teach them how to greet, and would command them to tranquillity and dignity in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), as in Sahih al-Bukhari and others, from Ibn al-Zubayr, when he spoke in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), his speech was not heard until he asked for it to be repeated.

It has been said that the meaning of "and do not speak to him loudly" etc. is: do not address him by his name or his kunya (teknonym) as some of you address others, but address him as "the Prophet" or "the Messenger." This interpretation is further from the appearance of repetition, but it contradicts the apparent sense, because the mention of loudness in relation to him does not clearly have a point; the apparent wording would have been, for example: "do not make your address to him like the address of some of you to others."

﴿Lest your deeds become void﴾. This is a reason for the two prohibitions that precede it, by way of the dispute over governance (al-tanāzuʿ), with a noun being understood: out of aversion that your deeds become void. The meaning is: I forbid you from what has been mentioned for fear that your deeds become void by committing it. Or it is a reason for the thing forbidden, namely raising and loudness, with the lām of cause understood: so that they become void. The meaning is that your doing what has been mentioned, for the sake of voiding, is forbidden. The understood lām of causation is used figuratively for the outcome to which the act leads, because raising and loudness are not for the sake of voiding, but they lead to it, as you will know, Allah willing. It has been distinguished between the two, the substance of which is that the forbidden act is the cause in the first, and the act that is the cause is forbidden in the second. Whichever is the case, the sense returns to this: that raising and loudness are both stated to lead to the voiding of deeds. The recitation of Ibn Mas'ud and Zayd ibn ʿAlI, "fa-taḥbaṭa" with the fāʾ, is more evident in stating that it leads to voiding, because what follows the fāʾ can only be caused by what precedes it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿while you do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of ﴿taḥbaṭa﴾, and the object of ﴿tashʿurūn﴾ is omitted, by the indication of what precedes it: that is, while you do not perceive that it is voiding. The apparent sense of the verse suggests that sins in general may void good deeds. The doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) is that the only thing that voids deeds is disbelief (kufr), and nothing else. The first view is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), and for this reason al-Zamakhshari said:

[p. 136]

"The verse indicates two dreadful matters: one of them is that by committing sins the believer's deed is voided, and the second is that among his deeds are some that one does not know are voided, though they may be voided in the sight of Allah, the Exalted."

Ibn al-Munir (may Allah have mercy on him) answered this, saying: the intent of the verse is a prohibition against raising the voice in an absolute sense, and it is known that the ruling of a prohibition is caution against what is anticipated from it in the way of harming the Prophet (ﷺ). The settled principle is that harming him (ﷺ) reaches the level of disbelief which voids the deed, by consensus. So the prohibition came against what is likely to lead to harming the Prophet (ﷺ), whether or not this meaning exists, as a protection of the means and a closing of the avenue. Then, since this prohibition is divided between what reaches the level of disbelief, namely that which harms him (ﷺ), and what does not reach that level, and there is no evidence distinguishing one of the two divisions from the other, it becomes binding on the responsible person to refrain from it altogether, for fear of falling into what voids the deed, which is what reaches the limit of harm, since there is no clear evidence distinguishing it. And if there were evidence, its distinction would not be achieved in many instances. The allusion to the confusion of one division with the other is made in His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿lest your deeds become void while you do not perceive﴾. Otherwise, if the matter were as al-Zamakhshari believes, His saying, may He be glorified, ﴿while you do not perceive﴾ would have no point, since the matter is confined between raising the voice being harmful, and thus definitively disbelief which voids, and being non-harmful, and thus, in his opinion, definitively a major sin which is voided. So in both states the voiding by it is established, and there is no point in qualifying the speech by non-perception, even though perception is established absolutely. Then he (may Allah have mercy on him) said: this estimation rests on two premises, both of which are sound. The first is that raising the voice is of the kind of thing by which harm is caused, and this is a matter attested by transmission and observation, to the extent that a teacher is harmed by a student raising his voice before him, so how much more so with the rank of prophethood and what it deserves of veneration and exaltation.

The second is that harming the Prophet (ﷺ) is disbelief, and this is established. Our imams have stated this explicitly and have issued rulings that whoever attacks this is to be executed as an unbeliever, and his repentance is not accepted. What he has done is greater in the sight of Allah, the Exalted, and more grave. End of quotation.

The sum of the answer is that there is no evidence in the verse for what al-Zamakhshari holds, because it may lead to voiding if it is done in a manner of harming or belittling. So He, mighty and majestic, forbade them from it and gave as its reason that it may void while they do not perceive. It has been said: it is possible, given the context, that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intends to raise the voice, it be treated as disbelief, as an intensification in honouring his assembly (ﷺ), and then there be applied to it what is applied to genuine disbelief, of voiding, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And for Allah, of the people, is the pilgrimage to the House﴾, up to His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then Allah is Free of need from the worlds﴾. The meaning of ﴿while you do not perceive﴾ in this view is: while you do not perceive that this is in the category of voiding disbelief, and it is not like other sins. And this does not hold without the first. It is also permissible, as in al-Kashshaf, that what is meant is what contains belittling, and this is from the category of ﴿So do not be a supporter of the disbelievers﴾, where the purpose is allusion. How much more so since this is a statement transmitted from al-Hasan, as al-Zamakhshari related it in al-Kashshaf. Abu Hayyan said: if the verse concerns one who does this out of belittling, then that is disbelief by which the deed is voided in reality. If it concerns the believer who does it out of heedlessness and habit, then what voids his deed is only the righteousness of honouring the Prophet (ﷺ) and lowering the voice in his presence, had he done that. It is as if it were said: lest the deeds that you are prepared to perform be voided, so that you would be rewarded for them. What is contained in this second part of the answer of artificial strain is not hidden.

Furthermore, there are kinds of loudness that the prohibition does not cover by consensus, such as what they did in war, or in disputing with an obstinate opponent, or in terrifying an enemy, or what is similar to that, which cannot be imagined as involving harm or belittling. In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib when the Muslims fled on the day of Hunayn: "Call out to the companions of the Samurah tree." So he called out with the highest of his voice: "Where are the companions of the Samurah tree?" He was a man with a loud voice. It is related that a raid came upon them one day, and al-ʿAbbas shouted, "O morning of ruin!" so that pregnant women miscarried because of the intensity of his voice. In this regard the poet Nabighah of Banu Ja'dah said:

"The shout of Abu ʿUrwah to the beasts of prey, when he feared they would mix with the sheep."

The narrators claim that he used to drive the beasts of prey away from the sheep, so that the gall bladder of the predator burst in its belly. It is mentioned that Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) was asked: "Then why does the gall of the sheep not burst?" He said: "Because they had become accustomed to his voice."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim related from Anas: when this verse was revealed, Thabit ibn Qays sat in his house and said: "I am among the people of the Fire," and he withdrew. The Prophet (ﷺ) asked Sad ibn Muʿadh, "O Abu ʿAmr, what is the matter with Thabit? Is he unwell?" Sa'd said: "He is my neighbour, and I know of no illness in him." So Sa'd went to him and said: "This verse has been revealed, and you know that I am the loudest of you in speaking before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so I am among the people of the Fire." Sa'd mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Rather, he is among the people of Paradise."

In another narration: when it was revealed, he entered his house, closed its door upon himself, and began to weep. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) missed him and said: "What is the matter with Thabit?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we do not know what his matter is, except that he has closed the door of his house and is weeping inside." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent to him, and asked him: "What is your matter?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah has revealed this verse to you, and I am of loud voice, so I fear that my deeds have become void." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You are not of them. Rather, you will live with goodness and die with goodness."

Apparently, that conduct from him (may Allah be pleased with him) was due to being overcome by fear, for otherwise there is no prohibition before the prohibition was revealed. Moreover, he is too exalted to be among those who intended to belittle and harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by raising their voices, and they are the hypocrites about whom the verse was revealed, according to what is narrated from al-Hasan. Rather, his raising of the voice was by natural disposition, since he had deafness in his ear, and it is the habit of many who have that condition to raise their voice. And it is apparent that after its revelation he abandoned this habit. Al-Tabarani and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) narrated that "Asim ibn 'Adi ibn al-'Ajlan informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of his condition, so he sent for him. When he came, he said: 'What makes you weep, O Thabit?' He said: 'I am loud-voiced, and I fear that this verse was revealed about me.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Are you not pleased to live praiseworthy, to be killed as a martyr, and to enter Paradise?' He said: 'I am pleased, and I will never again raise my voice above the voice of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'"

The scholars have derived from the verse the prohibition of raising the voice at his noble grave (ﷺ), and during the recitation of his hadith (ﷺ), because his sanctity after death is like his sanctity during life. Abu Hayyan mentioned the disliked nature of raising the voice also in the presence of a scholar. It is not far-fetched that it is forbidden when intended to harm or belittle, and that belittling anyone whose harming is forbidden is forbidden absolutely; but prohibitions have varying degrees, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 49, verse 3:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾ etc. is an encouragement to refrain from what they were forbidden, after a warning against violating it. That is, they guard it out of regard for courtesy, or out of fear of contravening the prohibition. ﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the relative pronoun, in view of its being characterized by what is in the relative clause; the sense of distance in it, despite the recency of reference to the one indicated, is for exalting his rank, as has been mentioned many times before. It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾, and the sentence is the predicate of "inna" (indeed). The root meaning of imtihan (testing) is trial and examination; what is meant here, since it is impossible to attribute it to Him, Exalted is He, is training, by way of the relation of necessity; that is, Allah Exalted has trained their hearts for piety. In al-Kashf it is said: "imtihan" is a suggestive metonymy for their patience in piety, their steadfastness in it, and their enduring its hardships, because the one who is tested has been tried and accustomed to the act again and again; it thus indicates the training that produces competence. Attributing it to Him, Exalted is He, serves to indicate enablement. Hence, according to what has been said, together with the metonymy there is a figurative usage in the attribution, and the original would be "they tested their hearts for piety by Allah Exalted's enabling them." It seems he considered this because the literal meaning intended here is not permissible, so it cannot be a metonymy according to those who require that the literal meaning be intended in it; whereas whoever is satisfied with the permissibility of the intention, even if it is impossible in the context of usage, does not need that consideration. Al-Shihab preferred that imtihan be a metaphor for patience, by way of the relation of necessity, and the resulting meaning on this is like its resulting meaning on the metonymy; that is, they are patient in piety, strong in bearing its hardships. Or the meaning of imtihan is knowledge, as is reported from al-Jubba'i, as a metaphor by way of mentioning the cause and intending the effect; the meaning is "Allah knew their hearts for piety." Attributing knowledge to Him, Mighty and Majestic, without the word itself is not impermissible, and it is common in the noble Qur'an. Moreover, the correct view is that attribution is permissible absolutely, because of the use in Nahj al-Balaghah of applying "al-'arif" (the knower) to Him, Exalted is He; and it has also come in a hadith, as some eminent scholars have claimed. The lam is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial phrase from "hearts": that is, existing for piety, specific to it. It is like the lam in the saying:

"And a polished ode, I have perfumed it; you are for it the most praiseworthy among mankind."

And his saying:

"Enemies of those who make the exhausted camels hasten over rough ground, and guests of the night who lodged for the descent."

Or it is connected to imtahana, in view of the meaning of habituation; or the meaning is that Allah Exalted struck their hearts with kinds of trials and arduous obligations for the sake of piety, that is, so that it might become manifest and it might be known that they are pious, since the reality of piety is not known except at times of trial and steadfastness upon it. On this view, imtihan is the striking with trials, and the lam is causal, in the sense that the manifestation of piety is the purpose and the cause; otherwise patience under the trial is derived from piety, not the reverse. Or the meaning is that He made it pure for piety, that is, made it sincere for the sake of piety, or made it purified for it, so that nothing of other than piety retains a right in it, as if the hearts became exclusively the property of piety; and this is more eloquent. It is a metaphor drawn from the testing of gold and its melting so that its pure essence separates from its impurity and is refined; or it is an analogy. The explanation of imtahana as akhlasa (purified) is related by Ibn Jarir and a group from Mujahid, and it is also reported from al-Ka'bi and Abu Muslim. Al-Wahidi said: the sense of the speech is "Allah tested their hearts and so purified them for piety," so "purification" was omitted, the testing indicating it. But this is not the case. Sahib al-Kashf preferred what was cited from him first, saying: "The first is the most preferred of the aspects, for the abundance of its benefit: from the metonymy, the attribution, and the indication that such lowering is not attainable except by one who is trained in piety and patient upon it. So reflect."

﴿For them﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿is forgiveness﴾ for their sins, ﴿and a great reward﴾ for their lowering their voices in the presence of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and for all their other acts of obedience. The indefiniteness of "forgiveness" and "reward" is for magnification; in describing the reward as "great" there is an emphasis on its greatness, for it is of what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human being. The sentence "for them" etc. is a resumed statement explaining the recompense of those who lower their voices, praising their condition, just as they were described by a sentence composed of two definites; the subject is the demonstrative which contains what was made a title for them, and the predicate is the relative clause with a relative sentence that shows their reaching the utmost perfection, as an emphasis on regarding their lowering and approving of it, and a rebuke against the ugliness of raising and loud voices, and that the condition of one who commits either is contrary to that. It is also said: the sentence is a second predicate of "inna", but this is not the case. It is said the verse was revealed concerning the two Shaykhs, may Allah be pleased with them both, because of what came from them of lowering the voice and of speaking with it in a hushed manner, after the revelation of the previous verse. And in the hadith of al-Hakim and others from Muhammad ibn Thabit ibn Qays that he said, after relating the story of his father and his saying: "I will never raise my voice again over the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him," and Allah Exalted revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾ the verse.

You know that its ruling is general, and the two Shaykhs enter into its generality, and likewise Thabit ibn Qays.

Ibn Mardawayh has indeed reported from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When Allah Exalted revealed: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: 'Among them is Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 49, verse 4 (part 1 of 2):

Those who call out to you from behind the chambers (﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ يُنادُونَكَ مِن وراءِ الحُجُراتِ﴾), meaning from outside them, behind them or in front of them. The word *wara'* (behind) is taken from *mu'awara* (concealment) and *istitar* (hiding). Whatever is hidden from you is *wara'*, whether behind or in front, so long as you do not see it. When you see it, it is no longer *wara'* for you. Thus, with respect to those inside the chambers, *wara'* is whatever lies outside them, because it is concealed from those within. Some lexicographers said that *wara'* is one of the *addad* (words with opposite meanings), in which case it is a *mushtarak lafzi* (homonym) with respect to the opposites, and a *mushtarak ma'nawi* (generic term) with respect to the first meaning. This is the view taken by al-Amidi and a group of others.

*Al-Hujurat* is the plural of *hujrah*, on the pattern *fu'lah* with a damma on the fa' and a sukun on the 'ayn. It is a piece of land enclosed (*mahjurah*, i.e. prevented from entry) by a wall. It is also called a corral for camels, the place where they are gathered and enclosed with wood or the like, and this too is called *hujrah*. It is thus in the sense of the passive participle, like *ghurfah* (a scoop) for what is scooped up by the hand of water. In its plural form here there are three readings: damma on the 'ayn, following the fa' (*hujurat*), as in the reading of the majority; fatha on the 'ayn, which is how Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read it; and sukun on the 'ayn for lightness, which is how Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it.

These forms are permissible in the plural of every solid noun that comes on this pattern. The intended meaning is the chambers of his wives (ﷺ). There were nine of them, each with a chamber. As Ibn Sa'd reported from 'Ata al-Khurasani, they were made of palm fronds, with coverings of black hair-cloth over their doors. Al-Bukhari in *al-Adab*, Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi reported from Dawud ibn Qays, who said: "I saw the chambers made of palm fronds, covered on the outside with hair-cloth. I think the width of the room from the door of the chamber to the door of the house was six or seven cubits, and I estimate the inner house to be ten cubits, and I think the height was between eight and seven."

They also reported from al-Hasan that he said: "I used to enter the houses of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) during the caliphate of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, and I would reach their roof with my hand. Then they were incorporated into the Mosque of the Messenger (ﷺ) during the reign of al-Walid ibn 'Abd al-Malik, by his order, and the people wept over this." Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said on that day: "By God, I wished they had left them as they were, so that some people of Madinah would grow up and the one who comes from the people of the distant lands would see what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was content with during his lifetime. That would discourage people from competing in and boasting about buildings." Abu Umamah ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf said something similar.

Mentioning *al-Hujurat* is an allusion (*kinayah*) to his (ﷺ) seclusion with his wives, since the chambers were prepared for them. He did not say "the chambers of your wives" or "your chambers", out of honour for him (ﷺ) and to avoid anything that would distress him (ﷺ). Their calling out to him from behind them may be because they came to the chambers one by one and called to him from behind them, in which case the intention is the customary comprehensiveness (*istighraq 'urfi*), i.e. all the chambers of his wives (ﷺ). Or it may be that they dispersed among the chambers seeking him (ﷺ). In that case the comprehensiveness is distributive (*istighraq ifradi*), not collective (*shumuli majmu'i*), and it is not a case of the plural being set against the plural, which would require the individuals to be divided among the individuals. For whoever called to him (ﷺ) from behind one of them has called to him from behind all of them, according to what has been said. On this view, the attribution of the calling is the attribution of the act of parts to the whole.

It has also been said that the one who called out was a single man, as is apparent from a report that al-Tirmidhi transmitted and graded as *hasan*, and from a group of others, from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib. And what Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted with a *sahih* chain, through Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from al-Aqra' ibn Habis: "He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, come out to us.' He (ﷺ) did not answer him. He said: 'O Muhammad, my praise is an adornment and my blame is a disgrace.' He said: 'That is God.' Then God revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you...﴾ and so on." On this view the attribution is to all of them, because they were content with it and ordered it, or because it occurred among them.

The apparent sense of the verse is that the callers were a group, and likewise a group is mentioned in the reports. We will mention some of them, God willing. Taking *al-Hujurat* as a true plural is the apparent meaning, and it is the view held by many of the exegetes. It is also permissible that *al-Hujurah* is singular, referring to the chamber in which the Messenger (ﷺ) was, and that it is pluralised out of reverence for him (ﷺ), following the style of "women other than you are forbidden to you". Also, his (ﷺ) chamber, being the mother of the chambers and the most noble of them, stands in the position of the whole, as in one of the two interpretations of God's words: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of God...﴾ (2:114).

Al-Zamakhshari distinguished between ﴿مِن وراءِ الحُجُراتِ﴾ with *min* (من) and *wara' al-hujurat* without it. He said that with the second form it is permissible for the caller and the one called to be behind the chambers together, but with the first form that is not permissible. He explained this by saying that *wara'* becomes a starting point of the goal (*mubtada' al-ghayah*) when *min* is added, and the same direction cannot be both a starting point and an endpoint for a single act. Abu Hayyan objected in *al-Bahr*, saying that the scholars explicitly stated, regarding the meanings of *min*, that it can denote both the starting point and the endpoint of a single act, and that one thing can be the locus of both. They attributed this to Sibawayh and said: among its examples is the saying "I took the dirham from Zayd", where Zayd is the locus of both the starting point and the endpoint of the taking together. They said: *min* is in most cases for the starting point only, and in some cases for both starting point and endpoint.

As for the author of *al-Taqrib*, his statement about it is open to examination. For the starting point and the endpoint are either the caller and the one called, which is the precise view, or the direction. If it is the first, then the *wara'* may combine both with *min* and without it, since the starting point and endpoint differ. If it is the second, then the direction is either divisible into parts or indivisible. If the first, then it is permissible to combine both with *min* as well, by considering the parts of the direction. If the second, then it is not permissible to combine both either with or without *min*, because the locus is one.

The reply to the first option is that the locus of the endpoint is the speaker alone, as Ibn Hisham mentioned in *al-Mughni*. It is also mentioned that Ibn Malik said that *min* in the example is for "passing beyond" (*mujawazah*). The second point does not undermine the distinction, according to what the author of *al-Kashf* stated. He said: "The summary is that the starting point is the direction, considered in terms of its being bound up with the agent, because the particle of beginning entered upon the direction, and the act is one whose meaning does not include distance. So both matters are taken into account, to fulfil the requirements of both the act and the particle. And since he made the whole direction a starting point, it could not be an endpoint, whether it is divisible or not. Then since *wara'* is undefined, it is not like 'I travelled from Basra to its mosque', since it is not determined which part of it is the starting point and which part the endpoint. Moreover, that too, when stated without qualification, must be understood to mean that the endpoint is other than Basra. But if it is specified, it is permissible with a figurative extension, and the original is its absence unless there is evidence. Then this permissibility applies where the endpoint is also a place. But if it is considered in terms of being bound up with the object, then it is not permissible. And if the particle of beginning is not mentioned, this meaning is not conveyed."

This is a genuine distinction. From this it becomes clear that the objection in *al-Taqrib* does not undermine it. What was mentioned, that the verifying view is that the act begins from the agent and ends at the object, and occurs in a location, and that ﴿مِن وراءِ الحُجُراتِ﴾ and *wara'aha* are both locatives, like "I prayed from behind the imam" (*min khalf al-imam*) and "behind him" (*khalfahu*), or "from before the day" (*min qabl al-yawm*) and "before it" (*qablahu*), and that the meaning of starting point is not verified, and the distinction is an evident artifice, reveals that *min* is superfluous, with no difference between its presence and absence. This is contrary to the apparent sense, for otherwise they would not have disagreed about its being superfluous in the affirmative form, given how common such speech is among them. And where it is not superfluous, there must be a distinction between the two statements, especially when both are from His words, the Mighty and Majestic. So reflect.

The expression of the calling in the present tense, although it preceded the revelation, is to bring the past scene vividly before the mind, because of its strangeness.

The relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) is the subject of *inna*, and the clause ﴿أكْثَرُهم لا يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ (most of them do not understand) is its predicate. The repetition of the predication is for emphasis. The meaning is that they do not act according to the requirements of reason, such as observing courtesy, especially with the most exalted of God's creatures and the greatest of them in God's sight, may He be glorified (ﷺ). The existence of a thing is often treated as its non-existence, for a reason. The judgement is made against most rather than all, because some of them did not intend to abandon courtesy, but called out for some purpose, according to what has been said. It is also permissible that the paucity indicated by the negation of the majority is meant as non-existence, since paucity is often used as a metonymy for non-existence. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that this applies to explicit paucity, not to what is understood from the negation of the majority.

These people were from Banu Tamim, as most historians of the biography of the Prophet (ﷺ) state explicitly.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A delegation of Banu Tamim came, seventy or eighty men, among them al-Zibriqan ibn Badr, 'Utarid ibn Hajib ibn Zurarah, Qays ibn 'Asim, Qays ibn al-Harith and 'Amr ibn al-Ahtam, to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in Madinah. 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn ibn Badr al-Fazari went with them, and he was always in every disturbance. They came to the dwelling of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and called out to him from behind the chambers with a harsh voice: 'O Muhammad, come out to us,' three times. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) came out to them. They said: 'O Muhammad, our praise is an adornment, and our blame is a disgrace. We are the most noble of the Arabs.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'You have lied. Rather, God's praise is the adornment, and His blame is the disgrace. And the most noble of you is Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim.' They said: 'We came to you to boast against you.' He mentioned it at length, and said at its end: 'The Tamimites said: By God, this man is one who has been prepared for this. His orator stood up and was more eloquent than our orator, and his poet recited and was more poetic than our poet.' And concerning them God revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers﴾, from Banu Tamim, ﴿most of them do not understand﴾."

This is the first reading.

Ibn Hisham, in his *Sirah*, reported from Ibn Ishaq the report at length, and counted among them al-Aqra' ibn Habis, and mentioned that he and 'Uyaynah had both witnessed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) the conquest of Makkah, Hunayn and al-Ta'if. He mentioned that 'Amr ibn al-Ahtam was behind the people in their rear, that their orator was 'Utarid ibn Hajib, and the orator of the Prophet (ﷺ) was Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, that their poet was al-Zibriqan ibn Badr, and the poet of the Prophet (ﷺ) was Hassan ibn Thabit. He mentioned the two speeches and what was said of poetry. When Hassan finished, al-Aqra' said: "By my father, this man is truly one to whom people come. His orator is more eloquent than our orator, his poet more poetic than our poet, and their voices are higher than our voices." When they had finished, they embraced Islam, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) rewarded them, and he gave their rewards generously. He also sent 'Amr his reward like the rest of the people. Ibn Hisham somewhat criticised the poetry.

In *al-Bahr* too there is a mention of the report at length, but in complete contradiction to what Ibn Ishaq related. In it: "Al-Aqra' stood up after al-Zibriqan had recited what he recited, and Hassan had replied with what he replied. He said: 'Indeed, by God, I came for a matter, and I have composed a poem, so listen to it,' and he said:

We came to you so that people would know our excellence,
when they oppose us in mentioning noble qualities.
We are the chiefs of the people from every group,
and there is none in the land of the Hijaz like Darim.
And for us is the quarter of every raid
that takes place in Najd or in the lands of Tihamah.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Hassan: 'Stand up and answer him.' He said:"

[Page 140]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 49, verse 4 (part 2 of 2):

O Banu Darim, do not boast; indeed your boasting will turn into a calamity at the mention of noble deeds.
May you be bereaved! You boast over us, while you are, for us, servants, between wet-nurses and attendants.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You were indeed, O brother of Darim, too ill-advised that there should be mentioned of you what you thought people had forgotten." His words (ﷺ) were harder on them than all that Hassan had said. Then Hassan returned to his poetry and said:

If you have come seeking to protect your blood and your property from being divided among the shares, then do not set up rivals to God, and submit, and do not boast before the Prophet of Darim.
Otherwise, by the Lord of the House, the spears will incline over your heads with the sharp, keen swords.

Page 142

Al-Aqra' ibn Habis said: "By God, I do not know what this matter is. Our orator spoke and their orator was better in speech, and our poet spoke and their poet was more eloquent and better in speech." Then he drew near to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "I bear witness that there is no god but God and that you are the Messenger of God." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "What has been before this does not harm you." End of quotation.

This is evident that al-Aqra's Islam was on that day. It is known that the year of the delegations was the ninth year, and that al-Ta'if and Hunayn had taken place before that. It has been mentioned from Ibn Ishaq that al-Aqra' witnessed both with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and it may be imagined from this that he was a Muslim at that time, which would contradict this. Rather, in the beginning and end of Ibn Ishaq's words there is something that gives the impression of contradiction. What is mentioned in the Sahihs is that he, and likewise Uyayna, were at that time among "those whose hearts are to be reconciled" (al-mu'allafa qulubuhum).

Ibn Ishaq himself narrated: "From Muhammad ibn Ibrahim, that a sayer among his companions said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of the distribution of what God had bestowed upon him on the day of Hunayn: 'O Messenger of God, you gave Uyayna and al-Aqra' a hundred each, and you left Ju'ayl ibn Suraqa al-Damri.' He said: 'By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, Ju'ayl is better than the full earth of such as Uyayna and al-Aqra'; but I reconciled those two so that they would become Muslims, and I entrusted Ju'ayl ibn Suraqa to his Islam.'" There has also come a marfu' report indicating that they were from Banu Tamim.

Ibn Mardawayh related through the route of Ya'la ibn al-Ashdaq from Sa'd ibn Abdullah: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the saying of God Most High: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you﴾ etc. He said: 'They are the rough ones of Banu Tamim. Were it not that they are among the people most fierce in fighting the one-eyed Dajjal, I would have prayed to God Most High against them that He destroy them.'"

In the Two Sahihs there is what testifies that they are among the most fierce of the Ummah against the Dajjal, and Abu Hurayra made this one of the reasons for his love for them. The apparent meaning of many reports is that the cause of their delegation was boasting. Al-Waqidi, who is a "night-gatherer of firewood" (hatib layl, i.e., one who gathers unreliable material), said: its cause was that they had raised weapons against Khuza'a, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent to them Uyayna ibn Badr with fifty men, among whom there was no Ansari or Muhajiri, and he took captive eleven men, eleven women and thirty children, and their chiefs were lost because of their captives. It is said that seventy or eighty men came from them on that account, among them Utarid, al-Zibriqan, Qays ibn Asim, Qays ibn al-Harith, Nu'aym ibn Sa'd, al-Aqra' ibn Habis, Riyah ibn al-Harith and Amr ibn al-Ahtam. They entered the mosque while Bilal had called the adhan for Zuhr and the people were waiting for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to come out to them, but these hastened and called out to him from behind the chambers, and there was revealed concerning them what was revealed. Then he mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave each man twelve ounces and a garment, and to Amr ibn al-Ahtam five ounces because of his young age. End of quotation. Perhaps the increase in his gift was because of what was said against him too, for Ibn Ishaq mentioned that Asim ibn Qays hated Amr and said: "O Messenger of God, there was a man among us in our households, and he is a youth, who speaks foolishly and disparages him." When this reached him, he said, addressing Qays:

You have sat spreading out the Halba, reviling me before the Messenger, and you were not believed, nor were you right.
We have led you in a calm leadership, and your leadership, its molars showing, sits upon sin.

It is narrated from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, that they were people of Banu al-Anbar; the Prophet (ﷺ) took captives from their offspring, so they came seeking their ransom, arrived at Medina, entered the mosque, and hastened for the Prophet (ﷺ) to come out to them, saying: "O Muhammad, come out to us." Al-Khafaji mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) sent a detachment to a group of the Arabs, who were Banu al-Anbar, whose commander was Uyayna ibn Hisn; they fled and left the women and offspring, so he took them captive and brought them to him (ﷺ). Their men came seeking the release of the captives, and called out from behind the chambers, so he (ﷺ) went out, released half, and ransomed the remainder.

The apparent sense of his words is that they were not from Banu Tamim, although this detachment may be identical with the one al-Waqidi indicated earlier. It is said that Uyayna in both accounts is Uyayna ibn Hisn ibn Badr, except that he is attributed there to his grandfather and here to his father. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 49, verse 5:

﴿If they had shown patience until you came out to them, it would have been better for them﴾. That is: if their patience and waiting until you came out had been steadfast, patience would have been better for them than hastiness, because it preserves good manners and the glorification of the Prophet (ﷺ), which earn praise and reward. Or (it would have been better) for that reason together with the granting of what they asked for in the most suitable and most agreeable manner for them, based on the hadith of the captives, namely that the Prophet (ﷺ) would release all of them without ransom. The anna (that) here, understood as a verbal noun (masdar), is the subject (fa'il) of a verb that is omitted, which is "thabata" (it was established), as preferred by al-Mubarrad. The context of the meaning points to this, since anna indicates establishment, and that occurs in the past in the strict sense; for this reason the omitted verb is taken to be in the past tense. The pronoun in kana (would have been) refers to the verbal noun indicated by "sabaru" (they showed patience), as in your saying: "Whoever lies, it would be worse for him", meaning, lying. The view of Sibawayh is that the verbal noun is in the position of the subject (mubtada'), so it is said that its predicate (khabar) is omitted, meaning, "if their patience were established". It is also said that it has no predicate. You know that in assuming the verb is omitted, "law" (if) remains in its literal sense of being followed by a verb, for it is originally a conditional particle specific to the verb. It is also permitted that the pronoun in kana refers to the verbal noun of the omitted verb, meaning, "the establishment of their patience would have been better for them". The practice of al-Zamakhshari suggests that this is the preferable view.

Hatta (until) is preferred here over ila (to), because hatta is used for what is an end in reality, which is called the "stipulated end" (al-ghayah al-madrubah), that is, the specified end, whereas ila is used for what is an end in reality or by the making of the one who makes it so. To this the view of the Maghariba (the grammarians of the Maghrib) and others refers: that the object of hatta, unlike the object of ila, must be the last part, as in "I ate the fish until its head", or must be adjacent to it, as in ﴿Peace it is until the rising of dawn﴾. One may not say, "I stayed up last night until its third or half". So the sentence with hatta conveys that their waiting until the Prophet (ﷺ) came out is a necessary matter, and it is not for them to cut off a matter before reaching it. Since Allah the Exalted made the coming out an end, it is so in reality. This is the view of al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Malik imagined that no one other than he had said this, and it was objected to with the line:

"I fixed a night, and I kept on, until its half, hoping, then I returned in despair."

It was answered that, even granting that it is from the speech of a reliable authority, together with its being rare and anomalous, an exception of this kind does not refute the rule. The rebuttal is that the meaning of "I fixed a night" is "I fixed a time for the visit", and it is customary that visits to loved ones take place at the beginning of the night. So his saying "until its half" explains the end of the time customary for visits, which is the beginning of the night, and the half is adjacent to it. This is better than the view of Ibn Hisham in al-Mughni that this is not a case of the condition, since he did not say "I remained in that night until its half", even though the meaning is based on it. The gist is that the condition applies specifically when the thing ended is explicitly mentioned, since there is no evidence for this restriction. And the obscurity of the insufficiency of placing "a night" at the beginning of the line is a matter to consider. Indeed, what has been mentioned of its basis is not free from discussion, as the statement of the author of al-Kashf indicates. For this reason, the more evident view says: it is more appropriate to use hatta takhruja (until you come out) for brevity, since anna must be omitted and ila requires it to be stated, while hatta is clearer in indicating the end appropriate to the ruling and the contrast between what follows and what precedes it. For this reason it is used to express cause, unlike ila. In His saying ﴿to them﴾ there is an indication that if he (ﷺ) came out not for their sake, it would be fitting for them to wait until he addressed them or turned toward them. So it is not superfluous, but a necessary restriction. ﴿And Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾, abundant in forgiveness and mercy. For this reason, glorified is He, He confined Himself to advice and rebuke for these wrongdoers who failed in good manners and neglected the honouring of His Messenger, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace. Yet it would have been appropriate for Him to punish them or destroy them, but the scope of His forgiveness and mercy, mighty and majestic is He, was not narrowed for these people if they repented and reformed. This is indicated by the saying of the Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, to al-Aqra', after he drew near to him, peace be upon him, and said: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah": "What harm is there to you in what came before this?" In the verses there is evidence of the ugliness of bad manners toward the Messenger (ﷺ) that is not hidden. From this and similar things the fruits of minds are gathered and the excellences of good manners are drawn, as is related of Abu Ubayd, and he was among the most virtuous, that he said: "I never knocked on the door of a scholar until he came out at the time of his coming out." Some have transmitted this from al-Qasim ibn Sallam al-Kufi. I saw in some books that the scholar Ibn Abbas used to go to Ubayy at his house to take the Noble Qur'an from him, and he would stop at the door and not knock on it until he came out. Ubayy thought this was a great matter for him, so one day he said to him: "Why did you not knock on the door, O Ibn Abbas?" He said: "The scholar among his people is like the Prophet among his community", and Allah the Exalted has said concerning His Prophet, peace be upon him: ﴿If they had shown patience until you came out to them, it would have been better for them﴾. I saw this story when I was young, so I acted in accordance with its requirement with my shaykhs, and all praise is due to Allah the Exalted for that.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mandah and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a sound chain (*sanad jayyid*), from al-Harith ibn Abi Dirar al-Khuza'i, who said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he invited me to Islam, so I entered it and affirmed it. He invited me to zakat, and I affirmed it. Then I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I will return to my people and invite them to Islam and to paying zakat. Whoever responds to me, I will collect his zakat, and you should send a messenger to me, O Messenger of Allah, at such and such a time, so that he may come to you with what I have collected of zakat.' When al-Harith had collected the zakat from those who responded to him, and the appointed time arrived, which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had intended to send [his messenger] to him, the messenger was delayed and did not come. Al-Harith thought that some displeasure (*sakhta*) from Allah and His Messenger, upon them be prayers and peace, had occurred concerning him. So he summoned the chiefs (*sarawat*) of his people and said to them: 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had set a time for me, when he would send his messenger to collect what we had of zakat, and the Messenger of Allah, upon him be prayers and peace, does not break promises. I do not see that his messenger has been held back except because of displeasure. So come, let us go to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.'

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'it, who was the half-brother of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, through his mother, to al-Harith, to collect what he had gathered of zakat. When al-Walid set out and reached part of the way, he became frightened and returned, and came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'Al-Harith withheld zakat from me and intended to kill me.' So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ dispatched a force (*ba'th*) to al-Harith. Al-Harith came out with his companions, and when he met them, having departed from Medina, they said: 'This is al-Harith.' When he approached them, he said to them: 'To whom have you been sent?' They said: 'To you.' He said: 'Why?' They said: 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqba to you, and he claimed that you withheld zakat from him and intended to kill him.' He said: 'No, by Him who sent Muhammad with the truth, I did not see him at all, nor did he come to me.' When al-Harith entered upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he said: 'Did you withhold zakat and intend to kill my messenger?' He said: 'No, by Him who sent you with the truth, I did not see him, nor did he see me, and I did not set out except when the messenger of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was delayed for me, fearing that it might be a displeasure from Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.' Then ﴿O you who have believed, if there comes to you a defiant one with news, investigate﴾ was revealed, until His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Wise﴾."

And 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from al-Hasan who said: "[A man] came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Prophet of Allah, the Banu so-and-so, a tribe of the Arabs, had something in his soul against them, and he was recently converted to Islam. They have abandoned the prayer, apostatized, and disbelieved in Allah, the Exalted.' The Messenger of Allah, upon him be prayers and peace, did not hasten, but summoned Khalid ibn al-Walid and sent him to them, then said: 'Observe them at the prayer times. If the people have abandoned prayer, then deal with them as you see fit, but if not, do not hasten against them.' So [Khalid] approached them at sunset, and lay in ambush until he heard the prayer. He watched them, and behold, the muezzin had stood at sunset, called the adhan, then gave the iqama, and they prayed the maghrib prayer. Khalid said: 'I see them only praying, so perhaps they have abandoned some other prayer.' Then he lay in ambush until, when the night grew dark and the twilight disappeared, their muezzin called the adhan and they prayed. He said: 'Perhaps they have abandoned another prayer.' He lay in ambush until, when it was the middle of the night, he advanced until the horses appeared at their dwellings. Behold, the people had learned some of the Qur'an, and they were performing the night prayer (*tahajjud*) with it and reciting it. Then he came to them at dawn, and behold, when the dawn broke, their muezzin had called the adhan and given the iqama. They stood and prayed. When they finished and the day had brightened for them, behold, the forelocks of the horses were in their homes. They said: 'What is this?' They were told: 'Khalid ibn al-Walid.' They said: 'O Khalid, what is your business?' He said: 'You, by Allah, are my business.' The Prophet ﷺ was told: 'You have abandoned prayer and disbelieved in Allah, the Exalted.' They fell on their knees weeping and said: 'We seek refuge in Allah, the Exalted, from ever disbelieving.' So [Khalid] turned the horses back from them, until he came to the Prophet ﷺ. And Allah, the Exalted, revealed ﴿O you who have believed﴾, the verse."

Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, even if it was revealed concerning these people specifically, it is sent (*mursala*) to the Day of Resurrection; nothing has abrogated it (*ma nasakhaha shay'*). But the earlier narration is more sound and more well-known. The statement of the author of *al-Kashf* explicitly states that the sending of Khalid ibn al-Walid was in the matter of al-Walid ibn 'Uqba, and that the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, sent him to those people of the tribe of Khuza'a after al-Walid's return and what he said. The one who holds this view said: 'They handed over the charities (*sadaqat*) to him, so he returned.' The address in the words of the Exalted ﴿O you who have believed﴾ includes the Prophet ﷺ and the believers of his community, both those who are perfect in them in good manners and others. Restricting the address according to what occurs of the command after it, since it suits the condition of some of them, does not remove it from generality, because it exists among them as well, so do not be heedless.

*Fasiq* (the defiant one) means one who has left the bounds of the Sacred Law, from the expression *fasaqa al-ratb* (the date came out of its skin, when it exits its husk). Al-Raghib said: 'Fisq (defiance) is more general than disbelief (*kufr*), and it occurs with a few sins and with many, but it has become customary for cases where they are many. And most often the term *fasiq* is applied to one who has committed himself to the ruling of the Sacred Law and affirmed it, then violated all its rulings or some of them. When the original disbeliever is called *fasiq*, it is because he has violated the ruling that reason imposed on him and that natural disposition (*fitra*) requires.'

Describing a human being with it, according to what Ibn al-A'rabi said, has not been heard in the speech of the Arabs. The apparent meaning here is that what is intended is a Muslim who violates something of the rulings of the Sacred Law or of *muru'a* (manliness and dignity), on the basis of its being contrasted with *'adl* (uprightness). Indeed, the absence of violating *muru'a* has been considered in *'adala* (moral integrity). The well-known view is to restrict its definition to violating something of the rulings of the Sacred Law, so do not be heedless.

*Tabayyun* is seeking clarification and knowledge of the matter, and close to it is *tathabbut* (verification), as in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i: ﴿fa-tathabbatu﴾ (so verify). It is seeking steadfastness and deliberation until the situation becomes clear.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada: "(The Prophet ﷺ said on the day the verse was revealed: Verification is from Allah, the Exalted, and haste is from Satan.)"

The indefiniteness of ﴿fasiq﴾ is for generality, because it is an indefinite noun in the context of a conditional, and an indefinite noun in the context of negation has the force of generality, as established in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul*). Likewise *naba'* (news), which, as in the *Qamus*, is "information." Al-Raghib said: "*Naba'* is not said of information in its original sense until it carries a great benefit, by which knowledge or a strong probability is obtained." And the words of the Exalted ﴿If there comes to you a defiant one with news, investigate﴾ are an alert that when the report concerns something great and of significance, it is required that one hold back in it, even if its soundness is known or strongly probable, until the matter is reexamined and thoroughly verified.

And since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and those with him were in a position where no one would dare to inform them of a lie, and the like of what al-Walid committed did not happen except rarely, [the verse] says ﴿If there comes to you﴾ with the particle of doubt (*in*). And in addressing them with ﴿O you who have believed﴾ there is an indication that if faith requires verification regarding the report of a defiant one, then it is more fitting that it requires the absence of defiance. And in excluding the defiant one from the address there is what indicates intensifying the matter against him, in the manner of "The adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer," and a believer does not lie.

The verse has been used as evidence that the defiant one is eligible to give testimony; otherwise there would be no benefit in the command to verify. Do you not see that when a slave gives testimony, his testimony is rejected and is not verified? This is contrary to al-Shafi'i.

It has also been used as evidence for the permissibility of accepting the report of a single upright reliable narrator (*khabar al-wahid al-'adl*), which the jurists of legal theory (*usuliyyun*) established on two grounds:

The first is that if his report were not accepted, the non-acceptance would not have been explained by defiance. This is because the single report on this assumption requires non-acceptance by its very nature, namely that it is a single report. So it is impossible to explain its non-acceptance by something else, since a ruling explained by its essence cannot be explained by something external. For if it were explained by something else, that would require its occurrence through that other thing, even though it already exists prior to it because it is explained by its essence, and this is void, because it would be obtaining what is already obtained, or it would entail two causes converging on one effect in the report of the defiant one. And the impossibility of explaining it by defiance is void because of the verse. If a ruling is attached to an appropriate attribute, it is strongly probable that the attribute is its cause, and probability suffices here because the aim is action. Thus it is established that the single report is not rejected, and if this is established, it is established that it is accepted and acted upon.

The second is that the command to verify is conditioned on the coming of a defiant one, and the implication of a condition (*mafhum al-shart*) is valid according to the correct view. Therefore it is obligatory to act upon [the report] when the reporter is not defiant, because probability is acted upon here. The view of an intermediate category is excluded.
