It has also been said that it refers to the flesh, and it has been said that it refers to the dead one, but this is not correct. It is permissible for it to refer to the backbiting understood from what precedes, and the meaning would be: "So hate it as you hate that eating." The past tense was used for emphasis. When it is interpreted as above, it becomes a command (inshâ') that does not require the implicit qad.

The accusative of ﴿dead﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) relating to either the flesh or the brother, because the mudaf (the first noun of the construct) is part of the mudaf ilayhi (the second noun), and a ḥāl is permissible in such a case, contrary to the view of Abu Hayyan.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, al-Jahdari, and Abu Haywa read ﴿fa-kurrihtumuhu﴾ with a ḍammah on the kāf and a shaddah on the rā'. Al-Khudri narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And fear Allah﴾ has been said to be a conjunction to an implied element, as if it were said: "Comply with what has been said to you, and fear Allah."

Al-Farra' said: The estimation is: "If that is true, then you have hated it, so do not do it, and fear Allah." So it is a conjunction to the implied prohibition. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: When it was said to them, ﴿Would any of you like...﴾ and so on, the answer was not specific, so it is as if they said, "We do not like it," and then it was said to them, ﴿then you would hate it﴾. It is estimated as: "Likewise, hate backbiting, which is its counterpart, and fear Allah," so it is a conjunction to the implied "hate." It has also been said that it is a conjunction to ﴿then you would hate it﴾ on the basis that it is a verbal report that is in meaning a command, as was previously indicated. The better opinion among these is not hidden.

His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance, Merciful﴾ is a justification for the command, meaning: because He, exalted is He, is Accepting of repentance and Merciful to whoever fears Him and avoids what He has forbidden and repents from what has passed from him. "Accepting of repentance" (tawwab) means intensive in accepting repentance. The intensiveness is either in terms of quality, since glorified is He makes the one who repents as one who has never sinned, or in terms of quantity, due to the abundance of those to whom repentance is granted, or due to the abundance of their sins.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi that Salman al-Farisi, may Allah be pleased with him, was with two men on a journey, serving them and receiving some of their food. One day he slept, and his two companions looked for him and did not find him, so they pitched the tent and said, "Salman wants nothing but this: to come to a prepared meal and a pitched tent." When Salman came, they sent him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to ask for some relish for them. He went and came to him and said, "O Messenger of Allah, my companions have sent me to ask you for relish, if you have any." He said, "What do your companions do with relish? They have already had relish." So Salman returned, may Allah be pleased with him, and informed them. They set out and came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said, "By He who sent you with the truth, we have not obtained food since we alighted." He said, "Indeed you two have had relish with Salman," and then this was revealed.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij that he said: "It is claimed that it was revealed concerning Salman al-Farisi, who ate and then slept, and then he was blown upon [in his sleep], and two men mentioned his eating and his sleeping, and so it was revealed."

Diya al-Maqdisi narrated in al-Mukhtarah from Anas, who said: "The Arabs used to serve one another on journeys, and with Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, was a man who served them. They both slept, then woke up, and he had not prepared food for them. They said, 'This man is very sleepy.' So they woke him and said, 'Go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and say to him: Abu Bakr and Umar send you greetings and ask you for relish.' He said, 'They have already had relish.' So they came and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, with what relish have we had?' He said, 'With the flesh of your brother. By Him in whose hand my soul is, I can see its flesh between your teeth.' They said, 'O Messenger of Allah, ask forgiveness for us.' He said, 'Tell him to ask forgiveness for you both.'"

This report is authentic, and there is no criticism of the two Shaykhs (Abu Bakr and Umar) in it, whether what occurred from them was before the revelation or after it, since they did not suppose, based on the good opinion of them, that this word was something that man would dislike.

This is what it is. The verse indicates the prohibition of backbiting. Al-Qurtubi and others have transmitted a consensus (ijma') that it is among the major sins (kaba'ir, the grave sins). Al-Ghazali and the author of al-'Uddah are reported to have stated that it is among the minor sins (saghair), and this is a surprising view from them, given how much indicates that it is a major sin. The most that has been said as a basis for the view that it is minor is that if it were not so, it would imply the sinfulness of all people except a rare individual, and this would be a great hardship. This has been answered: the spread of disobedience and the commission of it by all people, let alone most, does not necessitate that it is minor. What the statement indicates, namely that most people commit it, did not occur before. Moreover, persistence in it (iṣrār) is close to it in terms of its widespread prevalence among people, and persistence is a major sin by consensus, and this implies the great hardship, although it is not as great as the previous hardship. Furthermore, this argument does not withstand the many other proofs.

Perhaps the better argument for this is what Ahmad and others narrated with an authentic chain from Abu Bakrah, who said: "(While I was walking with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was holding my hand, and a man was on my left, we came upon two graves in front of us. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, they are being punished, and they are not being punished for something major,' and he wept... until he said: 'They are only being punished for backbiting and urine.')"

Yet this also is not conclusive. Ibn al-Athir said: The meaning is "they are not being punished for a matter that would be great for them and difficult for them to do if they had wished to do it," not that it is in itself not great. And how could it not be great when they are being punished for it? So the truth is that it is among the major sins. Yes, it is not far-fetched that some of it is among the minor sins, such as backbiting that does not greatly harm the person, like mentioning a flaw in clothing or a riding animal. And some of it should not be doubted to be among the greatest major sins, such as backbiting the awliya' (the friends of Allah) and the scholars with expressions of wickedness and immorality, and similar words that are very harmful. The more likely view is that the ruling on remaining silent about it, while able to prevent it, is the same as its ruling [i.e., it is equally prohibited].

The backbiter must hasten to repentance with its conditions: he must cease, and feel remorse, out of fear of Allah, exalted is He, so that he may free himself from the right of the one backbitten. Then he must seek the pardon (istihlal) of the one he backbit, so that he is freed from the injustice (maẓlimah). Al-Hasan said: Seeking forgiveness (istighfar) is sufficient instead of seeking pardon, and he cited the report: "The expiation for the one you have backbitten is that you ask forgiveness for him." Al-Khayyati issued a legal opinion that if it has not reached the one backbitten, remorse and seeking forgiveness suffice for him. Ibn al-Sabbagh affirmed this and said: "Yes, if his disparagement was among a people, he should return to them and inform them that it was not true." Many followed them, including al-Nawawi, and Ibn al-Salah chose it in his fatawa and elsewhere. Al-Zarkashi said: "It is the preferred view." Ibn Abd al-Barr narrated it from Ibn al-Mubarak, and that he debated Sufyan about it. What is used as evidence for the obligation of pardon is understood as an instruction toward what is better, or toward what entirely erases the trace of the sin immediately. As for what has been mentioned concerning the absent person and the dead, it is recommended that one ask forgiveness for them frequently. The pardon of the heirs has no weight, as Al-Khayyati and others stated. Likewise the child and the insane person, based on the correct view that backbiting them is forbidden.

Al-Khadim said: The correct view is that the right of claim of these two remains until the Day of Resurrection, meaning if pardon and forgiveness in this world are impossible, such as when a child dies as a child and an insane person dies insane. The right of Allah, exalted is He, is removed by remorse. Is it sufficient to seek pardon for backbiting that is unknown or not? There are two opinions. What al-Adhkar (of al-Nawawi) preferred is that it is necessary to know it, because a person may pardon one backbiting and not another. The words of al-Halimi and others require a firm decision that it is valid, because whoever pardons without revealing it has resolved himself to it, whatever the backbiting was. It is recommended for one who is asked for pardon to grant it, but it is not obligatory for him, because that is voluntary generosity and a favour from him. A group of the early generations (salaf) refrained from granting pardon, and my father, may Allah have mercy on him and be pleased with him, followed them, out of fear of treating the matter of backbiting lightly. The first view is supported by the report: "(Can any of you not be like Abu Damdam? When he left his house he would say: 'I have given my honour as charity to the people.')"

Its meaning is: I do not seek an injustice from them, and I do not dispute with them. It does not mean that backbiting becomes permissible, because there is a right of Allah in it, and because it is a pardon and permission for something before it becomes obligatory. Al-Ghazali was asked about backbiting a disbeliever and said: "Regarding a Muslim it is prohibited for three reasons: harm, belittling the creation of Allah, and wasting time on what does not concern one. The first requires prohibition, the second requires disapproval, and the third is contrary to what is preferable. As for the dhimmi (non-Muslim under the protection of the Muslim state), he is like the Muslim in what relates to the prohibition of harming him, because the Shari'ah has protected his honour, blood, and property."

Ibn Hibban narrated in his Sahih that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever makes a Jew or a Christian hear (something that harms him), for him is the Fire."

The meaning of "makes him hear" is to make him hear what harms him. There is no further discussion regarding its prohibition. As for the harbi (non-Muslim at war with the Muslims), his backbiting is not forbidden according to the first reason, is disliked according to the second, and is contrary to what is preferable according to the third. As for the mubtadi' (innovator), if his innovation amounts to disbelief, he is like the harbi; otherwise he is like the Muslim. As for mentioning him by his innovation, it is not disliked.

Ibn al-Mundhir said, regarding the Prophet's (ﷺ) explanation of backbiting: "(Your mentioning your brother with what he dislikes)." In this there is evidence that whoever is not your brother, among Jews, Christians, and all the other religious communities, and whoever his innovation has taken outside the religion of Islam, has no backbiting (protection against it). A similar reasoning applies to the verse. The correct view is the prohibition of backbiting the dhimmi, as has been established, and although it is not known from the verse or from the aforementioned report, it is known from another proof. There is no contradiction between what has been mentioned and that proof, as is not hidden. Backbiting may be obligatory for a valid legal purpose that cannot be reached except by it, and it is restricted to six causes.

The first: the one who has been wronged may complain to someone he believes has the power to remove the wrong, not merely to lessen it.

The second: seeking help to change an evil by mentioning it to someone who is believed to be able to remove it.

The third: seeking a legal ruling (*istifta'*). The one seeking a ruling may say to the mufti (jurist who issues rulings): "So-and-so wronged me in such-and-such a way. Is that permissible for him? Or what is the way to recover my right?" or similar. It is better, however, that he not name the person.

The fourth: warning the Muslims against evil, such as impugning witnesses, narrators, authors, and those who put themselves forward to issue fatwas or to teach recitation while lacking the qualifications. This is permissible by consensus (*ijma'*), indeed it is recommended. Likewise, one who is asked for advice, even if he was not consulted, may advise someone who intends to marry or to associate with another person in a religious or worldly matter, and he should limit himself to what suffices. If saying "It is not suitable for you" is enough, that suffices. If he needs to mention a defect, he mentions one defect or two, and so on. It is not permissible to add more than what suffices. Among this is that if one knows of a person in authority a flaw that disqualifies him, such as wickedness or heedlessness, it is obligatory to mention it to whoever has the power to dismiss him and appoint another who is free of it, or to advise him and urge him to uprightness.

The fifth: one who openly displays his wickedness, such as tax collectors (*makkasun*) and drinkers of wine in public. It is permissible to mention him for what they openly do, but not for anything else, unless there is another reason from those already mentioned.

The sixth: identification by a nickname (*laqab*) such as "the one-eyed" or "the blear-eyed." This is permissible even if he can be identified by something else. Yet it is preferable to avoid it if it is easy, and the aim must be identification, not disparagement. Most of these six are agreed upon, and they are supported from the Sunnah by sound hadiths mentioned in their proper places, such as the hadiths that indicate the ugliness of backbiting (*ghibah*) and the magnitude of its sins. Most people are addicted to it, and they say: "It is the soap of the hearts, and it has a sweetness like the sweetness of dates and an intoxicating craving like that of wine." In reality, as Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may God be pleased with them both, said: "Backbiting is the condiment of the dogs of people." We ask God Most High for success in what He loves and is pleased with.

How excellent is the order found in this verse, I mean His saying: ﴿O you who believe, avoid much of suspicion﴾, and so on. As Abu Hayyan said, and he explained it by saying: The command came first to avoid the path that does not lead to knowledge, which is suspicion. Then He forbade, secondly, seeking to verify that suspicion so that it becomes knowledge, by His saying: ﴿And do not spy﴾. Then He forbade, thirdly, mentioning it once it is known. These are three ordered matters: suspicion, then knowledge through spying, then backbiting.

Ibn Hajar, may God have mercy on him, said: God concluded each of the two verses with the mention of repentance, out of mercy for His servants and compassion toward them. But since the first began with a prohibition, it was concluded with a negation in ﴿And whoever does not repent﴾, because they are close to each other. Since the second began with a command in "avoid" (*ijtanibu*), it was concluded with it in ﴿and fear God﴾, and so on. The wisdom of mentioning the severe threat only in the first, by His saying ﴿And whoever does not repent﴾, and so on, is that what it contains is more vile, because it is harm done openly through mockery, insult, or nicknaming. This is unlike the second verse, for it is a hidden matter, since each of suspicion, spying, and backbiting requires concealment and generally the absence of knowledge of it. End of quotation. So do not overlook this.

[Page 162]

﴿O mankind, indeed We created you from a male and a female﴾, from Adam and Eve, peace be upon them both. Thus all people are equal in this, and there is no basis for boasting of lineage. From this is his saying:

People in the world of similitude are equals; their father is Adam and their mother is Eve.

It is also permissible that the intended meaning here is: We created each one of you from a father and a mother. But this is far-fetched, because the reproof of boasting of lineage does not appear to follow from it, while the discourse is directed toward that reproof, as what follows indicates. It was also said that it is a confirmation of the brotherhood which prevents backbiting, and the non-appearance of the consequence upon it remains as it is, although the fitness of what follows to it is less than its fitness to the previous interpretation. But the way in which it confirms brotherhood is evident.

﴿And We made you into peoples (shu'ub) and tribes (qaba'il)﴾. Shu'ub is the plural of sha'b, with a fatha on the shin and a sukun on the ayn, and it means a great multitude who trace their descent to a single origin. It encompasses the qaba'il (tribes). The qabila (tribe) encompasses the 'amA'ir (sing. 'imara, clans), and the 'imara, with a fatha on the ayn and sometimes with a kasra, encompasses the butun (sing. batn, sub-clans). The batn encompasses the afkhadh (sing. fakhdh, branches), and the fakhdh encompasses the fasa'il (sing. fasila, lineages). Thus Khuzayma is a sha'b, Kinana is a qabila, Quraysh is an 'imara, Qusayy is a batn, Hashim is a fakhdh, and al-'Abbas is a fasila. The peoples are so called because the tribes branched out from them. This is what most of the experts in genealogy and language hold. Some of the literati versified this, saying:

A tribe, above it a people, and after them the 'imara, then the batn which follows it, and the fakhdh.
A man finds shelter only with his fasila, and an arrow has no flight without its feathers.

Some of them mentioned the 'ashira (clan) after the fasila, saying:

Aim at the sha'b, for it is the most numerous group in reckoning, then the qabila.
Then follow them the 'imara, then the batn, then the fakhdh, and after it the fasila.
Then after them the 'ashira, but it is, in comparison with what we have mentioned, few.

Abu 'Ubayd related from Ibn al-Kalbi, from his father, the order: sha'b, then qabila, then fasila, then 'imara, then fakhdh. Thus he placed the fasila in the position of the 'imara and the 'imara in the position of the fasila, in mentioning them before the fakhdh, and he did not mention anything contrary to this.

It was also said: the shu'ub are the non-Arabs ('ajam), the qaba'il are the Arabs, and the asbat (tribes of descent) are the Children of Israel. What supports the view that the shu'ub are the non-Arabs is what is in the hadith of Masruq, that a man from the shu'ub embraced Islam and the jizya (poll tax) was being taken from him. The word shu'ub in it is interpreted as 'ajam. However, it has been said that its basis, as mentioned earlier, is that the sha'b is that from which the tribes of Arabs and non-Arabs branched out, so it was restricted to one of the two. It is also possible that it is the plural of shu'ubi, which is one who belittles the Arabs and does not consider them to have any merit over others, like the Jews and Magians in the plural of Majusi and Yahudi. Among them was Abu 'Ubayda, who was a Kharijite and who wrote a book on the faults of the Arabs, and Ibn Gharsiya, who has an eloquent treatise on the superiority of the non-Arabs over the Arabs, and scholars of al-Andalus refuted him with numerous treatises.

It was also said: the shu'ub are the Arabs of Yemen from Qahtan, and the qaba'il are Rabi'a, Mudar, and the rest of 'Adnan. Qatada, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak said: the sha'b is the more distant lineage and the qabila is the nearer lineage. It was also said: the shu'ub are the mawali (clients), and the qaba'il are the Arabs. Abu Rawq said: the shu'ub are those who trace their descent to cities and villages, and the qaba'il are the Arabs who trace their descent to their fathers.

﴿So that you may come to know one another (li-ta'arafu)﴾. Li-ta'arafu is the 'illa (cause) of the making, meaning: We made you thus so that some of you may know others, so that you may maintain the ties of kinship, distinguish lineages, and inherit, not so that you may boast of fathers and tribes. The restriction is derived from the specification by mention and the silence in the context of explanation.

al-A'mash read it as li-tata'arafu with two ta's, according to the original form. Mujahid, Ibn Kathir in one narration, and Ibn Muhaysin read it with the ta assimilated into the ta. Ibn 'Abbas and Aban, from 'Asim, read it as li-ta'rifu with a kasra on the ra, the imperfect of 'arafa. Ibn Jinni said: the object is elided, meaning: so that you may know what you are in need of, like his saying:

And He has taught man only so that he may know what He taught him. How sweet this omission is, and how strange it is for the one whose path is known.

Regarding the implied object, the nearness of some of you to others was chosen.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾, it is a reason for the prohibition of boasting of lineages, which is derived from the discourse by a true resumptive construction (istinaf haqiqi), as though it was said: Indeed the most noble of you in the sight of Allah, the Exalted, and the most elevated in rank before Him, the Mighty and Majestic, in the Hereafter and in this world, is the most righteous. So if you boast, then boast in righteousness.

Ibn 'Abbas read anna (with a fatha on the hamza) by eliding the lam of causation, as though it was said: Why do you not boast of lineages? It was answered: because the most noble of you in the sight of Allah, the Exalted, is the most righteous of you, not the one most noble in lineage. For the basis of the perfection of souls and the difference between persons is righteousness. So whoever seeks to attain the high ranks, let him hold fast to it.

In al-Bahr, it is related that Ibn 'Abbas read li-ta'rifu wa-anna akramakum with a fatha on the hamza. So anna akramakum etc. may be the object of li-ta'rifu, and the lam in li-ta'rifu would be the lam of command, which is better in meaning. But if the lam is the lam of kay (purpose), the meaning does not appear, since their being made into peoples and tribes is not for them to know that the most noble of them in the sight of Allah, the Exalted, is the most righteous of them. If it is taken as the object of li-ta'rifu elided, meaning so that you may know the truth, because the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you, then it is permissible for the lam to be the lam of kay. End. And it is, as you see, as it is.

﴿Indeed Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of you and your deeds, ﴿All-Aware﴾ of the inner states of your affairs.

It is related that when the Day of the Conquest of Mecca came, Bilal called the adhan (call to prayer) from atop the Ka'ba, and al-Harith ibn Hisham and 'Attab ibn Usayd became angry and said: Does this black slave call to prayer on the roof of the Ka'ba? So this was revealed.

And from Ibn 'Abbas, the occasion of revelation is: the statement of Thabit ibn Qays to a man for whom he had not made room near the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, "O son of such-and-such woman." The Prophet rebuked him and said: "Indeed you do not excel anyone except in religion and righteousness." And it was revealed.

Abu Dawud in his Marasil, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from al-Zuhri who said: "The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, commanded the Banu Bayada to marry a woman from among them to Abu Hind. They said: O Messenger of Allah, shall we marry our daughters to our freed clients? So Allah revealed: ﴿O mankind, indeed We created you from a male and a female﴾ the verse."

Al-Zuhri said: It was revealed specifically concerning Abu Hind, who was the cupper of the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him.

In the narration of Ibn Mardawayh, through al-Zuhri from 'Urwa, from 'A'isha: "He, peace be upon him, said: Marry Abu Hind, and marry to him. And ﴿O mankind﴾ the verse was revealed concerning that."

And from Yazid ibn Shajara: "The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, passed through the market of Medina and saw a black slave saying: Whoever buys me, on the condition that it not prevent me from the five prayers behind the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him. A man bought him, and the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, used to see him at every prayer. Then he missed him, and asked his companion about him, and he said: He has a fever. So he visited him. Then after some days he asked about him, and he said: He is in such a state. So he came to him while he was in his last breath, and he attended to his washing and burial. Then a great matter entered the Muhajirun and the Ansar." So it was revealed. There is some doubt regarding the soundness of this, and Allah the Exalted knows best.

It indicates that boasting of lineages is not proper, and the reports speak to this.

Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, and others related from Ibn 'Umar: "That the Prophet, peace be upon him, circumambulated on the Day of the Conquest on his riding-beast, touching the corners with his staff. When he came out he did not find a place to kneel, so he descended upon the hands of men and addressed them. He praised Allah, the Exalted, and extolled Him, and said: 'All praise is for Allah, who has removed from you the arrogance and pride of the Jahiliyya. O mankind, people are of two kinds: a pious, righteous one, noble before Allah, and a wicked, miserable one, lowly before Allah. All people are the children of Adam, and Allah created Adam from dust.' Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O mankind, indeed We created you from a male and a female﴾ until His saying, ﴿All-Aware﴾. Then he said: I say this statement of mine, and I seek forgiveness from Allah for myself and for you."

Al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Mardawayh related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: "The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, addressed us in the middle of the days of Tashriq, in the Farewell Sermon, and said: 'O mankind, indeed your Lord is One. There is no superiority of an Arab over a non-Arab, nor of a non-Arab over an Arab, nor of a black over a red, nor of a red over a black, except by righteousness. ﴿Indeed the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾. Have I not conveyed?' They said: Yes, O Messenger of Allah. He said: 'Then let the one present convey it to the one absent.'"

Al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Umama, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed Allah has removed the arrogance of the Jahiliyya and its pride in its fathers. All of you are from Adam and Eve, like the measure of a sa' equal to a sa'. Indeed the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you. So whoever comes to you, whose religion and trustworthiness you approve, then marry him." Ahmad and a group related something similar, but in it is not "whoever comes to you" etc.

Al-Bazzar related from Hudhayfa, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: "All of you are children of Adam, and Adam was created from dust. Let people cease boasting of their fathers, or else they will be more contemptible before Allah than dung beetles."

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet, peace be upon him, who said: "Allah will say on the Day of Resurrection: O mankind, I made lineage, and you made lineages. I made the most noble of you in My sight the most righteous of you, but you refused, except that you say: So-and-so son of so-and-so, and so-and-so is nobler than so-and-so. Today I raise My lineage and lower your lineages. Indeed My friends are the righteous." Al-Khatib related from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, something similar, traced to the Prophet.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, Abu Ya'la, al-Baghawi, Ibn Qani', al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Abu Rayhana that the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever traces his lineage to nine disbelieving fathers, desiring by them honor and pride, he is the tenth of them in the Fire."

Al-Bukhari and al-Nasa'i related from Abu Hurayra, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, was asked: Who among people is the most noble? He said: The most noble of them before Allah is the most righteous of them. They said: We are not asking you about this. He said: Then the most noble of people is Yusuf, the Prophet of Allah, son of the Prophet of Allah, son of the Friend of Allah. They said: We are not asking you about this. He said: Then are you asking me about the mines of the Arabs? They said: Yes. He said: The best of them in the Jahiliyya are the best of them in Islam, when they comprehend."

The hadiths on this topic are too many to be counted. In the verse there is an indication of the reason for rejecting boasting of lineage, in that it conveys that the nobility of lineage is not acquired. ﴿And that there is for man only what he has striven for﴾. Also, there is no difference between the kin and others in terms of the substance, since both were created from the same thing, nor in terms of the agent, since it is Allah the Exalted, the One. So lineage has no nobility upon which one may rely, and which would be the basis of reward before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. No one is nobler than another before Him, glory be to Him, except by righteousness, and by it the soul is perfected and persons are distinguished. This does not contradict the Arabs being nobler than the non-Arabs, nor the variation of each of the Arabs and non-Arabs in nobility. They have mentioned that the Persians are nobler than the Nabateans, and the Children of Israel are superior to the Copts.

Muslim and others related from Wathila ibn al-Asqa', who said: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed Allah chose Kinana from the descendants of Isma'il, chose Quraysh from Kinana, chose from Quraysh the Banu Hashim, and chose me from the Banu Hashim." This is only by consideration of praiseworthy qualities, for the nobility of the Arabs over the non-Arabs, for example, is only by consideration that Allah, the Exalted, distinguished them over others with numerous virtues and praiseworthy qualities, as the hadiths have confirmed. Among those who gathered many of them is the scholar Ibn Hajar al-Haytami in his book Mablagh al-Arab fi Fada'il al-'Arab. We do not mean by this that every Arab is distinguished over every non-Arab by praiseworthy qualities, but rather that the whole is distinguished over the whole. Furthermore, the noblest of the Arabs in lineage are the descendants of Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, because they are traced to the Prophet, peace be upon him, as a group of jurists have stated explicitly.

[Page 165]

And al-Tabarani narrated from Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: (The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every descendant of Adam is affiliated with a 'asabah (paternal kin group) except the children of Fatimah. I am their wali (protector) and I am their 'asabah.")

In another report of his, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: "(Every son of a woman has his 'asabah (paternal kin) as his father, except the children of Fatimah. I am their 'asabah and I am their father.)" The authenticity of this has been disputed. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti graded the first report as hasan (good), and this was criticised. The matter does not rest on what has been mentioned, because its evidence is clear.

Ahmad and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak narrated from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, and there is no objection to it (its chain is sound). He said: (The Prophet ﷺ said: "Fatimah is a part of me (bid'atun minni). Whatever pains her pains me, and whatever gladdens her gladdens me. Indeed all lineages will be severed on the Day of Resurrection except my lineage, my sabab (means/cause of connection), and my marital relation (sihr).")

The hadith of Fatimah being a part of the Prophet (bid'iyyat Fatimah), may Allah be pleased with her, is also recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari. al-Sharif al-Samhudi said: It is well known that her children are a part of her, so through her they are a part of him ﷺ. This is the utmost honour for her children. The fact that his ﷺ lineage is not severed also appears in a hadith narrated by Ibn 'Asakir from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, raised (to the Prophet ﷺ), with the wording: (Every lineage and marital relation will be severed on the Day of Resurrection except my lineage and my marital relation.)

Although al-Dhahabi criticised it by saying that Ibn Wakī' is in its chain and that it should not be relied upon, he compensated for this by saying that a good mursal (a report whose chain omits a companion) also came through it. From what has been mentioned, and what is similar to it, as al-Manawi said, the great benefit of affiliation to him ﷺ becomes clear. This is not contradicted by what appears in other reports of his ﷺ urging his household to fear Allah and guard against Him, and that he ﷺ would not avail them anything before Allah, out of his eagerness for their guidance and his warning them not to rely on lineage, lest their steps fall short of joining the foremost of the God-conscious. Thus they would combine two nobilities: the nobility of piety and the nobility of descent. Out of regard for the station of warning, he ﷺ addressed them with his words: (I cannot avail you anything against Allah.)

The meaning is: I cannot avail you anything by my own self alone, apart from what Allah honours me with, such as intercession for you and forgiveness from Him, the Exalted, for you. He ﷺ does not possess benefit or harm for anyone except by Allah's granting him possession of it. Allah, the Glorified, grants him the benefit of his ummah, and the nearest kin are more deserving of kindness.

Based on this, there is no harm in a man saying: "I am from the descendants of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ," in the manner of speaking of a blessing or other lawful purposes. al-Manawi transmitted from Ibn Hajar that he said: The Prophet ﷺ's prohibition against boasting of lineages applies where the boasting entails arrogance and the belittling of a Muslim. In accordance with what we mentioned at first, his ﷺ saying (Indeed Allah chose Kinanah from among the sons of Isma'il) comes, and so on. His ﷺ saying: (I am the Prophet, there is no lie; I am the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib) and so forth.

Despite the nobility of being affiliated to him ﷺ, it is not fitting for one whom Allah has granted it to leave it devoid of piety, and to defile it by following desire. A good deed in itself is good, and when it comes from the house of prophethood it is even better. An evil deed in itself is evil, and when it comes from the people of the house of prophethood it is worse. The following of desire may reach the point where a person with this noble ancestry is ashamed to be attributed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and may even deny his lineage. For this reason it was said to a noble man of bad conduct:

"The Prophet said a true saying that has never ceased
to be sweet to hearing and to mouths.
If a man's origin is lost to you, his deeds
reveal to you his origin, which is exalted.
And I see you revealing deeds that have never
been without equal among people.
You say: 'I am of the lineage of Ahmad.'
Are you the one who speaks truly, or is it the Messenger of Allah?"

A noble man deserves no blame except for himself when he is then treated in a way he dislikes, and someone far lower than him in lineage is given precedence over him. It is related that a certain sharif in the land of Khurasan was the nearest of people to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but he was a manifest sinner. There was a black freedman there who was advanced in knowledge and practice, and people crowded to honour him. It happened one day that he left his house heading to the mosque, and a great multitude followed him seeking blessing from him. The sharif met him while intoxicated, and the people were trying to push him away from the road. He overpowered them, clung to the edges of the shaykh's garments, and said: "O black one of the hooves and lips, O unbeliever son of an unbeliever! I am the son of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, I am humiliated while you are honoured, and I am disgraced while you are assisted!" The people intended to beat him, but the shaykh said: "Do not do this. He is to be tolerated for his grandfather, and pardoned even though he has exceeded his limit. But, O noble one, I whitened my inner self and you blackened yours. The whiteness of my heart appeared above the blackness of my face, so I became beautiful, and the blackness of your heart appeared above the whiteness of your face, so you became ugly. I took the conduct of your father and you took the conduct of my father. So people saw me in the conduct of your father and saw you in the conduct of my father, and they thought I was your father's son and thought you were my father's son. So they treated you as one treats my father, and treated me as one treats your father."

For this, and similar reasons, it was said:

"Lineage from Hashim does not benefit
if the self is from Bahilah."

That is: lineage does not benefit in gaining distinction over those with praiseworthy qualities if the self is in itself Bahili, base, and devoid of perfections. Bahilah was originally the name of a woman from Hamdan who was married to Ma'n ibn A'sar ibn Sa'd ibn Qays 'Aylan, and her son was attributed to her. It is also said: the Banu Bahilah are a people known for baseness. It is said that they would eat the leftover food a second time, and would take the bones of carrion, boil them, and take their grease. The Arabs belittled them greatly, to the extent that it was said to an Arab: "Would you accept being a Bahili and entering Paradise?" He said: "No, unless it is on condition that the people of Paradise do not know that I am a Bahili." It was also said:

"When it is said to the dog, 'O Bahili!'
the dog howls from the ill omen of this lineage."

The jurists did not make them equal (kafa', compatible for marriage) to other Arabs for this reason. However, this is not free from scrutiny, for the text, namely (The Arabs are kafa' to one another), was not qualified, although the Prophet ﷺ was most knowledgeable about the tribes of the Arabs and their characters, and it was stated without restriction. Not every Bahili is as they say; rather, among them are the generous. That a branch or clan of them acted as they did does not apply to all of them. Unless it is said:

The basis of kafa'ah (compatibility) and its absence rests on shame and its absence among what is known among people. So when they regard Bahilah as shameful, and its belittlement spreads among them, and their souls reject it, then this is taken into account, even if it does not stem from a noble origin. This is similar to what the jurists mentioned concerning a person who buys a house and it becomes clear that people regard it as unlucky: he has the option (of cancelling the sale), despite the view of the majority of scholars denying the conventional ill omen among people, taking into account that this lowers the price among people even if it has no basis. So reflect on this.

In sum, nobility of lineage is considered both in the pre-Islamic era and in Islam. As for the pre-Islamic era, it is too evident to need proof. As for Islam, it is indicated by the consideration of kafa'ah in lineage in the chapter on marriage, in the detail given in the books of jurisprudence. Apart from Imam Malik, al-Thawri, and al-Karkhi of the Hanafis, we know of no one who disagreed on this. Some of what has preceded of the reports supports their words, but we answer that in its proper place. Likewise, what the jurists mentioned in explaining the conditions of the Great Imamate (the supreme leadership of the Muslim community) indicates this: that its conditions require that the Imam be from Quraysh. They reached consensus on this, as al-Mawardi said. No account is taken of the dissent of Dirar and Abu Bakr al-Baqillani, for they departed from consensus by permitting it for all people. The Shafi'is said: If no Qurashi is found, that is, one who combines the conditions of the Imamate, then it is required that the Imam be a Kinani, from the descendants of Kinanah ibn Khuzaymah. If that is impossible, then it is required that he be from the sons of Isma'il, peace be upon him. If that is impossible, then it is required that he be from Jurhum, because of their nobility through marriage with Isma'il, peace be upon him, and so on.

Despite all of this: piety, piety. Relying on lineage while abandoning the self and its desires is a sign of weak judgement and little intellect. The statement of Allah, the Exalted, to Nuh, peace be upon him, concerning his son Kan'an, suffices in this matter: ﴿He is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose deeds are unrighteous﴾.

And his ﷺ saying: (Salman is of us, the people of the House.)

So the fitting prudence for the noble is to fear Allah, the Exalted, and to acquire praiseworthy qualities which, if they were found in one who is not noble, would suffice him, so that he adds sweetness to the butter and places a necklace upon the neck of the beautiful. He should not be satisfied with mere affiliation to forefathers who passed away, so that it is said to him: "What excellent forefathers, but what bad successors they left!" Many people have been afflicted with this. You see one of them boasting of a decayed bone while he is bare, like a needle, of every perfection. He says: "My father was such and such," and that is a description of his father. His boasting in it is like the boasting of the beardless one with the beard of his brother.

From here it was said:

"The most astonishing thing to a wise person
is a people who have held back from excellence,
when asked what glory they possess,
they point to a bone that is decayed."

Al-Fadil al-Sari 'Abd al-Baqi Efendi al-'Umari said:

"I say to one who every time
boasts to us of great ancestors:
Are you content with bones, while you know
that the dog is content with bones?"

How elegant is his saying:

"Lofty lineage has not benefited you without piety;
so beware and fear Allah, your Master."
"Seek honour in attaining glory through it,
for the most honourable of people before Allah are the most pious."

Most of the time we have seen this cold boasting among the children of the shaykhs of the Sufi lodges. They commit every vice and are stripped of every virtue, yet they boast of their fathers over the excellent of creation, and they belittle people who surpass them in lineage and nobility of father and mother. This is manifest error and a folly beyond which there is no further. Were it not for fear of tedium, we would let loose the reins of the swift pen in this field. Yet in what we have mentioned there is sufficiency for one whom providence has taken by the hand. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 49, verse 14:

﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed."﴾ Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning the tribe of Banu Asad ibn Khuzayma, a tribe living near Madina. They professed Islam while their hearts were corrupt; they only loved spoils and the goods of this world. It is also related that they came to Madina in a year of drought, professed the two testimonies (shahadatayn), and used to say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We have come to you with our belongings and our dependents, and we did not fight you as Banu so-and-so fought you." By mentioning this they meant charity, and they conferred a favour upon the Prophet (peace be upon him) by it. It was also said: they were Muzayna, Juhayna, Aslam, Ashja' and Ghifar. They said, "We have believed," so they deserved honour, and Allah the Exalted rejected this from them. Whatever the case, the intended meaning of "the Bedouins" is not generality, as Qatada and others have explicitly stated. The attaching of the feminine marker to the verb (qalat, rather than qala) is due to the prevalence of treating plurals as feminine, to the extent that it was said:

"Do not care for their gathering; every gathering is feminine."

The point of treating it as feminine here is to indicate the weakness of their intellects, in contrast to what is observed in His saying: ﴿And the women said﴾.

﴿Say: you have not believed﴾ is a refutation of their claim to faith, since faith is assent together with certainty and tranquillity of the heart. This was not present in them; otherwise they would not have placed the Messenger (ﷺ) under obligation by refraining from fighting, as the end of the surah indicates. ﴿But say: we have submitted (aslamna)﴾, for islam is submission and entry into peace (silm), which is the opposite of war, and what these people had did not suggest that. The apparent wording would have been "you have not believed, but you have submitted," or "do not say, 'We have believed,' but say, 'We have submitted'," so that the correspondence (mutabaqa) would be achieved. However, the wording departs from the apparent form, being content with the correspondence being achieved in meaning, together with the incorporation (idmaj) of additional benefits. The explanation of this is that the purpose for which the speech was framed is to rebuke these people for their claim of favour through their faith: they were devoid of it at first, and if they were truthful, they would be the ones conferring favour. Thus the basic form of guidance regarding their answer would have been: "Say, you have lied." But it was expressed as what was actually revealed, in order to convey that the attribution of lying is not confronted directly. This also entails that the Prophet (ﷺ) is directed toward courtesy in the matter of everyone, so that it becomes a habit for his followers, and so that they do not wear the tiger's skin when addressing someone. The summary of what they lied about is as follows.

Among the evidence that this is the basic form is His saying in the following verse: ﴿Those are the truthful ones﴾, which is an implicit indication that lying is confined to them. This was preferred over "do not say, 'We have believed'," because such a statement is objectionable, especially from the Prophet (ﷺ), who was sent to call to faith. Moreover, the conveying of "you have not believed" in the sense of "you have lied" is clearer than the conveying of "do not say, 'We have believed'," as is not hidden. Then it is contrasted with His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿But say: we have submitted﴾, as if it were said: "Say, you have not believed, so do not lie, but say, 'We have submitted', so that you may attain truthfulness if faith and assent have escaped you." Had it been said, "But you have submitted," this meaning would not have been conveyed. In it there is an allusion that their submission, which is void of assent, is not regarded as valid. Had it been said, "But you have submitted," it would have suggested that this is regarded as valid, whereas what is sought is its perfection through faith. This does not need to be answered by saying that the saying here is used in the sense of claiming (za'm). It was also said that there is ihtibak (a rhetorical device where parts omitted from each of two parallel clauses are supplied by the other) in the verse. The original would be: "You have not believed, so do not say, 'We have believed', but you have submitted, so say, 'We have submitted'." So from each of the two clauses was omitted what was mentioned in the other. The first form is more eloquent and subtler.

﴿And faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (qulu, "say"), as if it were said: "Say, 'We have submitted,' as long as you are in this state." In it there is an indication of the expectation that faith will enter their hearts later. Therefore this negation is not a repetition of His saying: ("you have not believed"). It was also said that the clause is independent (mustanafa), and there is no repetition either, because lamma (لَمّا) conveys negation extending continuously from the past up to the present time by consensus, and it conveys that what it negates is expected, contrary to Abu Hayyan. Lam (لَمْ), on the other hand, conveys none of that without disagreement. So there is no need, in removing the repetition, to say that it is circumstantial, or to make the clause a time-limit for the command to speak.

﴿And if you obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ with sincerity and abandonment of hypocrisy, ﴿He will not deprive you (la yilitkum) of any of your deeds﴾, meaning He will not diminish for you ﴿anything﴾ of their rewards, or any of the diminishment. It is said: lataho yalituhu latan when he diminished it. From this is what al-Asma'i related from Umm Hisham al-Sulamiyya: "Praise be to Allah, who is not overtaken, nor diminished, nor are voices deafened to Him." Al-Hasan, al-A'raj and Abu 'Amr read (la ya'iltukum), from alata ya'ultu, with the lam vowelled with damma and kasra, as alatan. This is the dialect of Asad and Ghatafan. Al-Hutay'a said:

"Convey to the nobles of Banu Sa'd a message, delivering the effort of the mission, neither diminished nor false."

The first form is the dialect of the Hijaz, and the verb in it is hollow (ajwaf, with a weak middle radical). In the second form the initial radical is hamzated (mahmuz al-fa', having a hamza as first radical). Abu 'Ubayda related: alata yalitu. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾ of what was neglected by the obedient, ﴿Merciful﴾ in bestowing bounty upon them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 49, verse 15:

﴿Only those are the believers who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, and then have not doubted.﴾ "Lam yartabu" means they did not become doubtful. Irtaraba is a reflexive form (mutawi') of raaba, meaning that he caused him to fall into doubt when there was suspicion (al-tuhma). Making the absence of doubt come after faith, although it is never separated from faith, serves to indicate the negation of doubt in what follows, when a dubious matter befalls them. It is as if it were said: they believed, and then there did not befall them what befalls the weak after some time. This does not indicate that they were doubtful at first. Rather, it indicates that just as they did not doubt at first, no doubt arose in them afterwards. The summary is: they believed, and then no doubt arose in them, so the sequence is temporal (zamani). Some of the eminent scholars said: the conjunction of the absence of doubt to faith is of the type of (His angels, and His messengers, and Jibril), to draw attention to the fact that it is the essence of faith, as if it were something else, higher than it, present within it. The particle "thumma" (then) was preferred over the conjunction "waw" (and) to indicate that this essence is, in its newness and its oldness, equal in strength and steadfastness. So it is always in its freshness, not that it is one continuous thing, which would make it like a fixed object. Rather, it is renewed and fresh from time to time. There is no harm in regarding it as tarshih (a rhetorical reinforcement) of what the meaning of the conjunction indicates. When it is treated as distinct, it is noted that it is not a difference between continuity and occurrence, but the difference between two different things, so as to indicate the meaning mentioned and that they are increasing in certainty moment by moment. As for those who say that faith admits of strength and weakness, this is evident. As for those who do not say so, it is due to the joining of direct observation to explanation. The difference between the two kinds of continuity is that continuity in the first sense is the continuity of the whole, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They say: Our Lord is Allah, then they stood firm﴾, meaning that their faith continued with that, along with the absence of doubt. In the second sense, continuity is considered in the last part only. This latter view is more preferable. In any case, there is an allusion (ta'ridh) in the speech to those Bedouin Arabs.

﴿And they strove with their wealth and their selves in the way of Allah﴾, that is, in His obedience, may He be exalted and glorified, through the multiplicity of its kinds of acts of worship: the purely physical ones, the purely financial ones, and those that combine both, such as Hajj and jihad. Placing wealth before selves is by way of tarraqqi (ascent from the lower to the higher). It may also be said that He placed wealth first because of the great greed people have for it, to the extent that they destroy themselves on its account. This is more suitable from the viewpoint of the allusion to those Bedouins, since it was not enough for them that they did not strive with their wealth, until they came, or displayed Islam, out of love for spoils and the goods of this world. The meaning of "jahadu" (they strove) is that they exerted effort, or its object is understood as implied: the enemy, or the self and desire. ﴿Those﴾, who are described by what has been mentioned of beautiful qualities, ﴿they are the truthful﴾, that is, those who were truthful in their claim of faith, not those Bedouins. It is reported that when this verse was revealed, they came and swore that they were believers and truthful, so He revealed this to refute them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 49, verse 16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Will you inform Allah of your religion?﴾ That is, will you inform Him, glory be to Him and exalted, of that by your saying, "We have believed." ﴿Tu'allimuna﴾ (you inform) is derived from ʿalimtu bihi (I knew of it), so it is transitive by doubling (taḍʿīf) to one object directly and to the second by means of the preposition (ḥarf al-jarr). It was said that it takes the preposition because it has been made to imply the meaning of encompassing (iḥāṭa) or perceiving (shuʿūr), which gives it added emphasis, inasmuch as it operates like something perceived by the senses. His exalted saying: ﴿And Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the object of ﴿tu'allimūna﴾, and in it is a rebuke of their ignorance that is not hidden. His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyīl) that confirms what came before it, meaning: He is thorough in knowledge of all things, among which is what they concealed of disbelief while displaying belief.

﴿They consider their Islam a favor to you.﴾ That is, they count their Islam as a favor (minnah) to you. A minnah is a benefit whose giver seeks no reward from the one he confers it upon. The word al-mann here carries the sense of cutting off, because its purpose is to cut off the recipient's need. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: it is a heavy blessing, from *al-mann* by which something is weighed. Its heaviness is its magnitude, or the hardship in bearing it.

The clause ﴿أنْ أسْلَمُوا﴾ (*an aslamu*, "that they embraced Islam") is in the position of the object of *yamunnuna* (they confer favor), because the verb is taken to imply the meaning of *i'tidad* (counting something as a favor), which is the process of *tadmin* (implicit meaning, where one verb is given the sense of another). Alternatively, the preposition is understood, so the verbal noun is in the accusative by removing the preposition (*naz' al-khafid*), or in the genitive by the understood preposition. The meaning is: they confer favor upon you by their Islam. The same may be said of His words: ﴿Say: Do not confer favor upon me by your Islam.﴾ Its meaning is either: do not count your Islam a favor upon me, or: do not confer favor upon me by your Islam.

Abu Hayyan permitted that ﴿أنْ أسْلَمُوا﴾ be an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), meaning: they show grace to you for the sake of their Islam.

﴿Rather, God confers favor upon you that He guided you to faith.﴾ That is, (guided you to faith) in what you claimed by your saying "We have believed." This does not contradict His words: ﴿Say: You have not believed.﴾ Or, guidance here means merely general indication (*mutlaq al-dalalah*), so it does not necessarily imply that they have faith, and it does not contradict the earlier denial of faith.

Abdullah and Zayd ibn Ali read ﴿إذْ هَداكُمْ﴾ (*idh hadakum*, "since He guided you") with *idh* being causal (*ta'liliyyah*). It was also read ﴿إنْ هَداكُمْ﴾ (*in hadakum*) with *in* being conditional (*shartiyyah*). ﴿If you are truthful.﴾ That is, in your claim of faith. Thus the truthfulness is connected to the claim, not to the guidance, so do not be heedless of this. The response of the condition is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, meaning: then God's favor is upon you.

The delicacy and elegance of the context of this verse are not hidden. Those Bedouins were called, by God, Islam, to expose their lie in their saying "We have believed." That is, the thing that came about was Islam, presented in the context of bestowing favor. He, glorified be He, denied that what they claimed was faith. When they conferred favor upon the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, for what they had done, He, glorified be He, said to His Messenger, peace be upon him: They count upon you with something not worthy of being counted, namely their talk, which deserves to be called Islam only. So say to them: Do not count your Islam as a favor upon me, that is, your talk which is called Islam by me, not faith. Then He, exalted be He, said: Rather, God counts as a favor upon you that He has strengthened you with His success, in that He guided you to faith, according to what you claim. In His words ﴿your Islam﴾ with the genitive construction there is an indication that this is not something to be counted, and that it is something befitting such people, so how could it be made a favor? He, Mighty and Majestic, did not attach the word faith (*iman*) to them, to alert that the intended faith is the faith that is worthy of being counted. Glorified be He, by His words, exalted be He: ﴿If you are truthful﴾ He drew attention to the fact that this is a lie from them. The subtlety lies in placing the denial first

Then the answer concerning the favour (al-mann), while observing the subtleties in each of these, and the completeness of the beauty lies in the concluding phrase (al-tadhyil, a closing statement that reinforces the meaning of what precedes it) with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning what is hidden in them, ﴿and Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, meaning in your secret and in your open conduct. So how could what is in your inner selves be hidden from Him, glorified is He? This is to show their lie, and to show that He, Mighty and Majestic, makes His special servants aware of it: the Prophet (ﷺ) and his followers, may Allah be pleased with them. Ibn Kathir and Aban, from Asim, read (ya'malun) with the ya of the third person. And Allah knows best.

From the mode of allusive interpretation (al-ishara, esoteric indication) in some of the verses: ﴿O you who believe, do not put forward [anything] before Allah and His Messenger﴾, and so on, is an indication of the necessity of acting in accordance with the Sharia, observing good manners, and abandoning the demands of the natural disposition (al-tab'). His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, if a defiantly disobedient person brings you a report, then verify it﴾ indicates that if the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammara bi al-su', the soul that incites to evil) prompts and brings a report of one of the desires of this world, it is necessary to be cautious, in order to ascertain its profit and its loss, ﴿lest you harm a people﴾, meaning from among the hearts and their attributes, ﴿out of ignorance, and then become﴾ on the morning of the Day of Resurrection ﴿regretful for what you have done﴾. For that which contains the healing and life of the souls contains in it the sickness and death of the hearts. ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah﴾, and so on, points to the messenger of divine inspiration (ilham rabbani) in the souls, by which He makes them aware of their wickedness and their piety. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If one of the two groups transgresses against the other, then fight the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of Allah﴾ indicates that when the soul wrongs the heart by the domination of its desires, it must be fought until it is wounded by the swords of striving (al-mujahada), and if it responds with obedience, it is pardoned, for it is the mount to the gate of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your two brothers﴾ is an indication of observing the right of religious brotherhood. Its source is the loins of prophethood (sulb al-nubuwwa), and its reality is the light of Allah, Exalted is He. So reconciling between them means removing the veils of the coverings of human nature from the faces of the hearts, so that the light may join with the light through the aperture of the heart, and they become as one soul. ﴿O you who believe, let not a people ridicule [another] people, perhaps they may be better than them﴾ indicates abandoning self-admiration and looking upon anyone with the eye of contempt, for the outward appearance is not regarded by Him, and the inward is not known to anyone. How many a dishevelled, dust-covered one with two worn garments, who if he swore by Allah, Allah would fulfil it! His saying: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed"﴾, to the end of it, contains an indication that one should abandon seeing one's own deeds, and know that the favour in guidance belongs to Allah, the King, the Exalted. In it is also guidance on how to address the ignorant and how to respond to those who are veiled, as the indication to it has already passed. This, and we ask Allah for success in what pleases Him on the Day of Presentation before Him.
